## WHAT IS CONTAINED
### in this volume.

I. A correction of those who, without <term>philosophical study</term> <note>In this context, "philosophical study" refers to the deep theoretical understanding of nature's laws, which alchemists believed was necessary before attempting physical experiments.</note>, attempt to reap the fruits of the alchemical art.

II. A book on the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note>, called the *Clang of the Trumpet* <note>original: "Clangor Buccinæ"</note>.

III. A brief and concise treatise on the <term>vegetable stone</term> <note>original: "lapide uegetabili"; Alchemists categorized their materials into mineral, animal, and vegetable "stones" or essences.</note>, which the Philosopher called the *Path of the Path* <note>original: "Semitam Semitæ"</note>.

IIII. A short treatise by *Avicenna* <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works were foundational to medieval European alchemy, though many works attributed to him were later deemed "pseudo-Avicenna."</note> on the <term>tincture</term> <note>An elixir or agent used to "dye" or transform the properties of a metal.</note> of metals.

V. The *Compendium of the Soul* of transmutation, sent to *Rupert, King of the English* <note>Likely referring to a legendary or misidentified monarch, as Raymond Lull’s works were often dedicated to high-ranking patrons to lend them authority.</note>, by *Raymond* <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many alchemical texts were attributed.</note>.

VI. The book called the *Ladder of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Scala Philoſophorum"; This title suggests a step-by-step guide to the stages of the alchemical process.</note>.

VII. *The Work of Women* <note>original: "Opus mulierum"</note>, a short treatise, or *Children’s Play* <note>original: "ludus puerorum"; These are common alchemical metaphors suggesting that once the "Stone" is understood, the actual work is as easy as household chores or games.</note>.

VIII. *Raymond Lull’s* compendium on Tinctures.

IX. *Aristotle’s* short treatise on the practice of the Philosopher’s Stone. <note>Like Avicenna, Aristotle was often cited as an authority in alchemy, though the works were usually written by later medieval authors using his name.</note>

That very essence which gives life to and produces all things, being enclosed within its own boundaries in the most noble and perfect metals, he attempted to capture through art. By then applying this to the more serious diseases of the human body, he—to great acclaim—vanquished many illnesses that were even considered incurable. Those who have a fresh memory of the matter report that not long before these times, there was a certain Theophrastus of Transylvania <note>The author likely refers to Paracelsus's travels or a confusion regarding his origins; Paracelsus was actually Swiss, but his fame spread throughout Eastern Europe.</note> who, having grasped the deeper mysteries of this art, discovered a substance which those ancient philosophers and searchers of nature undoubtedly intended to signify through their parables and veils. # THE CORRECTION
## OF FOOLS, A TRULY
### USEFUL AND AUTHENTIC LITTLE
### treatise begins happily.

#### *Prologue to the same book.*

Since the correction of all things is their very augmentation <note>The author argues that "correcting" a substance—purifying or altering it—actually increases its inherent power or value</note>. Therefore, it is written in many sayings of the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" usually refers to ancient alchemists like Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle</note>, that nature is corrected through art beyond the movement it possessed in its primary form. For no art can labor except by the mediation of nature, since nature herself works intrinsically and secretly within the art through the administration of the craftsman. From this it follows, that the imitation of nature is the increase and labor of virtue <note>original: "uirtutis," referring here to the inherent power or "essence" of a substance</note>, and the augmentation of the thing itself; for nature completes its own degree, which it can naturally fulfill, and it cannot pass beyond that unless it is hindered by an opposite force. However, art does not truly transcend nature by creating a new nature through simple labor.
<margin>How art imitates nature</margin>
And for this reason it is said that art imitates nature, not that it builds a new one, but that it refines the power of that nature. Because of this, art begins to perfect where nature fails—namely, to uncover the subtle nature enclosed within a thing, and to make it manifest.

<summary>This introductory page establishes the alchemical principle that human art does not replace nature, but rather assists and perfects it by uncovering hidden virtues that nature alone cannot release.</summary>

## ON THE UTILITY OF STUDY.

Study removes ignorance and leads the human intellect back to true knowledge and to the science of any thing whatsoever. Therefore, it is necessary above all else to acquire knowledge through the study of this sweet work, and to sharpen the wit through physical sayings <note>original: "phyſica dicta" – likely referring to the writings of natural philosophers or "physicists" in the Aristotelian sense</note>, since the knowledge of truth is contained within them. If, therefore, those who labor do not despise study, they shall sweetly taste the fruit resulting from it. But those who shrink from study, and yet wish to labor, let them see whether their art is an imitation of that nature which the art itself ought to improve. For it is impossible for such a person to prepare the secrets of the philosophers to a perfect end. Concerning these people, the wise say that they proceed to practice just as a donkey goes to dinner, not knowing toward what they stretch their snout, except insofar as the exterior senses—without intellect—lead them to their fodder through sight and taste. Thus these "donkeys," being without true good principles and fruitful studies, and

# ON THE NATURAL
# PRINCIPLES
## OF THIS ART. CHAPTER
->The First.<-

There is no doubt that this art possesses true principles, since nature itself forms metallic bodies from minerals. <term>Uñ</term> <note>Latin: "Unde," meaning "Whence" or "Therefore."</note> <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher whose theories on the four elements and the formation of minerals provided the scientific foundation for alchemy.</note> in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*, distinguishes mineral bodies into stones, sulfurs, and salts; and some of these are rare and proud <note>Likely referring to "noble" or "brittle" qualities</note>, and some of them are ductile <note>Capable of being hammered thin</note>, while others are not. And what the reasons and causes of their generation are is made clear in that same place. Therefore, it is not necessary to say more about them here.

### How many parts of minerals there are.
->Chapter II.<-

Mineral bodies are specifically distinguished into two parts: namely, the metallic part and the mineral part. Into the metallic part—that is, into the metals which derive their origin from Mercury <note>In alchemy, Mercury is considered the "mother" or fluid principle of all metals.</note>. And into the mineral part, which does not draw its origin from Mercury. Of the metals, examples are Gold, the Moon <note>Silver</note>, Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>, Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, Mars <note>Iron</note>, Saturn <note>Lead</note>, and electrum <note>A natural alloy of gold and silver</note>. Such as salts, inks <note>original: "atramenta," likely referring to vitriol or dark pigments</note>, alum, vitriol, arsenic, and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, as opposed to those metals which draw their origin from Mercury. All metals that originate from Mercury are both ductile <note>capable of being hammered thin</note> and liquefiable, because their matter is an aqueous substance mixed with an earthy substance by so strong a bond that one cannot be separated from the other. Therefore, that aqueous substance is congealed more by cold after the action of heat, and they will thus be ductile or workable by a smith. Water alone is not congealed except by an earthy dryness which alters the wateriness; since the moisture in these metals is not oily, and because their solidification comes from earthy dryness, they are not easily dissolved except by the action of vehement heat upon them, according to how strongly or very strongly they are mixed.

### *On the generation of Mercury and which metals are generated from it. Chapter IV.*

Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> in its first root is composed of a white, subtle, excessively sulfurous earth, strongly mixed with clear water, until it becomes a single substance that does not rest on a flat surface, nor does it adhere to what touches it, by reason of the dryness which has altered the wateriness within it. # CORRECTION

It is stable and airy, and this is the sign of perfection. And therefore, when it first flows through the sulfurous earth while heated, it ascends to the higher parts. Hence its nature is such that it is refined by heat. Nevertheless, through continuous sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> it is excessively purified, cooked down, and thickened; and through white and red sulfur, it is gradually congealed. Since sulfur is dissolved many times, the sublimated quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> is first coagulated and softened like wax by the action of heat, until—scarcely over thousands of years in the successive work of nature—it is coagulated into a perfect metal. Indeed, within these mineral vessels, nature itself works the metals. In these works, therefore, it is necessary to imitate nature for whoever wishes to perfect a medicine <term>Medicina: In alchemy, this refers to the "Elixir" or "Tincture" capable of transforming base metals into gold or healing the body</term> from imperfection to perfection. Although the bodies themselves differ in their composition from the quicksilver from which they are generated, they do so according to whether that mercury was pure or impure, and whether it came from clean or unclean sulfur. For if quicksilver is coagulated from pure sulfur in which there is a power of fieriness, it will be simple gold. If, however, the sulfur was bad and weak, and the Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; used here interchangeably with quicksilver</note> was of good substance, it converts it into copper <note>original: "æs"; can refer to copper, bronze, or brass</note>. But if the quicksilver was heavy, earthy, and impure, and the sulfur was impure, foul-smelling, earthy, and of a fixed substance, iron is made from it, which afterwards is not easily melted. Tin, however, is seen to have good quicksilver, shin—

Artificers are able to perform congelations <note>The process of turning a liquid into a solid</note> through these means—that is, to extract the moisture from Mercury with dry substances so that the Mercury appears coagulated—but that coagulation is of the worst kind. Whence Aristotle says: "Let the Alchemists know that they cannot truly change the species of things, but they can make things similar to them." That is, they can tint a red substance with yellow so that it appears to be gold, and tint a white substance with whatever color they wish until it becomes very similar to silver. This is done by those who join together tin, copper, and Mercury, and from these make a sophisticated <note>In this context, "sophistic" means counterfeit or artificial</note> silver. A purification of metals through minerals is also performed, and this is not impossible; reason does not stand against these things. However, regarding true gold and silver, it is by no means granted that they can be made in nature or by art, except through the reduction of bodies into their "first matter" <term>First Matter: the formless, original substance from which all things are created</term>. In this way, the species of things can be transmuted, as Aristotle previously added. And this is not achieved by simple melting alone, but by the resolution of coagulated Mercury; when the body is transformed into Mercury through the admixture of its own spirit.

### Question.

Since the Philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle, the standard authority in medieval science</note> speaks generally, saying that sulfur coagulates, it must be said that it does not. For all common sulfur, according to the Philosopher, is foreign and contrary to metals. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician and alchemist</note> says: *That which did not originate from it does not enter into the mastery* <note>original: "Non intrat in magisterium quod non est ortum ab eo" - meaning only substances of a metallic nature can be used to transform metals</note>. For it always infects, blackens, and corrupts, in whatever way it may be prepared by artifice. For it is itself an infected fire, and therefore it hinders fusion. If indeed it is calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, it returns into an earthy substance, like a dead dust. In what way, therefore, can it inspire life in others? For it possesses a double superfluity: namely, an inflammable substance and an earthy dross.

### Chapter VII.

But because in the preceding chapter it was determined that it is impossible for the lesser minerals <note>original: "minora metalla," often referring to mineral salts or non-metallic ores like vitriol or alum.</note> to be made into metals artificially, it remains here to be proven. # OF FOOLS

The first part of the preceding argument is clear: that the lesser metals <note>referring to base minerals or ores like vitriol or alum</note> are not generated from Mercury. The reason for this is that Mercury always remains in the "first matter" of metals, and does not contain foreign sulfurs. Hence, Aristotle and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician and philosopher</note> state: Therefore, if metals were to be made, it would be necessary for them first to pass into the first matter of metals. But because this cannot be done artificially, metals can by no means be made from them. Thus, the first part of the preceding statement is sufficiently declared.

Secondly, regarding the same point: Because the lesser minerals cannot be artificially made into the principle of metals—which is Mercury—they likewise do not reach the middle or the <margin>Against strong waters <note>original: "Contra aquas fortes"; likely referring to corrosive acids used in attempts to dissolve minerals</note></margin> end, which are the metal itself and the tincture <term>tincture: a transformative substance or color-giving essence</term> which it holds. This is because nourishment in a human being cannot become a human through generation unless it is first converted into sperm; thus, when added to its like, a new human is generated. But because the lesser metals are of a nature foreign to true metals—even though they participate well enough in some mineral power—they are of a weaker virtue and are combustible <note>original: "adustibilia"; prone to being burnt away or oxidized</note>. Therefore, the metallic nature does not rejoice in them, but rejects them, and preserves those things <margin>A beautiful comparison</margin> which are of its own nature. For example: if water is mixed with earth, they are separated from one another, because the earth seeks the bottom since it is heavy and dry, while the water seeks <margin>understand that nature is not made except from the elements <unclear>of the sun and gold</unclear></margin> the surface. In no way can they be so joined artificially that these contrary natures remain as one.

<margin>What yellowing is.</margin>
Yellowing <note>original: "citrinatio"; the alchemical stage where the matter turns from white to gold</note> is nothing other than complete digestion. For heat acting upon moisture first generates blackness, and acting upon dryness it causes whiteness; if the heat transcends this, acting further upon that whiteness, it changes it into the purest yellow. All these things can be observed in the calcination <note>the process of heating a substance until it reduces to powder</note> of lead. Also, the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: because each of the perfected bodies already contains its own good sulfur with Mercury in actuality—namely, gold contains golden sulfur, and silver contains silvery sulfur. Therefore, white sulfur [turned] through yellow is gold. For this reason, the sulfur within it is red sulfur, that is, the substance of fire, which has further digested this white. And thus, white and red sulfur exist on both sides within the Sun <note>original: "sole"; the alchemical symbol for Gold</note>. Wherefore fire is its perfection, and it is generated in fire; and therefore, nature amicably rejoices in its own fiery nature. Hence, external things cannot cause this in the bodies, since art—with nature mediating—is nothing other than the decoction <note>boiling down</note> and digestion of that nature through simple labor. For example: in the morning when I rise and see my urine is white, I judge that I have slept too little; then I lay myself down again to sleep, and having taken more sleep, the urine becomes yellow. And this is on account of the greater digestion of the natural heat existing within me. Thus, follow nature through art in a similar way: to boil, to digest, and to mature substantially, since nature already contains within itself the natural fire in actuality.

<margin>The Rule</margin>
You could, however, purge metals with lesser minerals; yet even when purged, they still do not possess a golden or silver nature within themselves. This is because the golden digestion and decoction <note>term: decoction (the process of "ripening" or "cooking" a substance over heat to reach perfection)</note> was not present in them as it was in others, nor was their sulfur so mature. And therefore, these immature things must be aided by mature ones so that they may be ripened. Thus, they do not tint <note>original: "tingunt" — to dye or transform the essence of a metal</note> but are themselves tinted, because the tincture of gold and silver has a nature proportionate to them—namely, to the immature or imperfect—because they drew their origin from Mercury. From these things it is clearly evident that lesser minerals cannot perform the transformation, because imperfect metallic bodies which do not agree with gold and silver on the part of mature Mercury cannot transform, nor can they infuse the nature of gold or silver. And therefore, one must not attempt to transform except with those things in which the power of transforming resides. Transform, therefore, with gold and silver, because gold bestows a golden color and nature. For this reason, you should despise all other things which do not virtually or naturally possess the power of transformation, since in them there is no fruit, but only the ruin of things and the gnashing of teeth.

# THE CORRECTION

Since gold <term>aurum; the most perfect metal in alchemy</term> is held by both common people and Philosophers to be the highest form, remaining in its primary disposition, it may cure leprosy and possess many other virtues. This is due to its complete digestion <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the process of maturing or refining a substance through heat, mimicking natural growth</note>, because the excellence of the fire acting within it consumes all evil humors existing in sick bodies, whether arising from a hot or cold cause. 

However, silver <term>argentum</term> cannot do this, because it does not possess such a superfluity of fire, nor is it as digested and cooked by natural maturity. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, it possesses a fiery nature hidden and virtual within it, but not so fully, because as of yet the fire has not produced such elemental qualities as are found in gold. And therefore, silver remaining in its primary disposition does not cure leprosy so powerfully, unless it is first digested by art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy, which seeks to accelerate natural processes</note> until it attains the highest degrees of gold in all maturity. 

For this reason, other sick metallic bodies cure infirmities even less, according to how much they differ in imperfection and maturity from these, and due to the defect of infected, foul, and burning sulfur <term>sulphur; one of the two primary principles of metals, often associated with impurity when "foul"</term> from which they were made by their generation and coagulation from the beginning; and therefore they do not cure. Since gold is of such great vigor among common people, even while remaining in its primary disposition, it is no wonder—as has been proven by experience—if gold is reduced into medicines through the ministry of art following nature, and its virtue is made subtle through the digestion of cooking and quality.

## On the Nature of Mercury. Chapter XVIII.

Know that Mercury—whether within the earth through the work of nature, or outside of it through the work of art—will never come to, nor remain in, union with any body unless it is "mortified" <note>In alchemy, "mortification" refers to the process of changing a substance's outward form or "killing" its metallic life to prepare it for transformation.</note> and restrained. It is mortified <margin>The coagulation of Mercury.</margin> and restrained through proper sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again.</note>, and through the soaking of sharp waters <note>Likely acids or corrosive liquids.</note>, and the "feeding" of metal filings pertaining to it. Especially through the vapor of sublimated and prepared sulfur, it is led and coagulated into a metallic hardness and form. <margin>Into metallic form</margin> Its most sublime "food" is white marcasite <note>A term used historically for various iron sulfides or bismuth.</note> for the white work, and red for the red work. Know that this has been proven; therefore, be cautious and experienced in its sublimation. For I have seen that when it is sublimated in a glass vessel with a long neck prepared for this purpose, it always remains the same no matter how often it is sublimated; it is not dried further, nor hardened, nor does it have a vent at the top through which its vanishing and watery moisture might fly away. However, when in sublimation or among its other preparations it begins to become "glandular" <note>original: "glandosus," likely referring to the formation of small, nut-like kernels or beads.</note>, then know that it is already being converted into the species which you intend. <margin>Glandular Mercury</margin> Observe it according to this, and you proceed on the right path in the work. This last chapter is ascribed to Callisthenes <note>A reference to the pseudo-historical alchemical authority often cited in medieval texts.</note>.

And note that there are four elements, namely fire, air, water, and earth. This is because each of them is composed of two primary qualities, and no more: such as fire from heat and dryness, air from heat and moisture, water from cold and moisture, and earth from cold and dryness. Furthermore, heat in fire is its essential quality <note>The defining characteristic</note>, while dryness is its accidental quality <note>A secondary characteristic that can change without the substance losing its identity</note>. In air, moisture is its essential quality, but heat is accidental. In water, moisture is its principal or essential quality, but coldness is its accidental quality. In earth, dryness is its principal beginning or essential quality, and coldness is accidental. Likewise, fire is properly hot and dry by its property. For heat is greater in a thing when it comes from its qualities than when it comes from its property. Understand the other qualities of the elements in this same way.

Regarding the origin of the four elements, Myretis <note>Likely a reference to a legendary alchemical authority or a corruption of a name like Hermes or Mary the Prophetess</note> says: Know that earth was formerly water, then turned into stone and made rocky; water was formerly air, then it was liquefied and thickened and turned into water; however, the beginning of air was fire, because it came from thickened fire. Fire, truly, lacks a beginning, except for its Creator.

And we speak of the grades of those elements: because fire, as it exists in a mixture, is hot in the fourth degree and dry in the third degree.

<margin>The less pure part, that is, 5 parts</margin>
Because the supreme Creator divided that less pure part into five parts. From one part, which was the purest, God created the **fifth essence** <term>quintessence: the purest, celestial element that exists beyond the four earthly elements</term>, the substance of the elements, which shares in the nature of heavenly things. And this He divided into four parts: The first and purest is given to **fire**, which God created from the second part of the nature of the elements; the second pure part is attributed to **air**, which was created from the third, less pure part of the nature of the elements; and the third, less pure part is given to **water**, which is the element created from the fourth, less pure part of the nature of the elements; and the fourth, less pure part is given to the **earthly element**, which was created from the fifth and least pure part of the whole nature of the elements. And the less perfect a nature is, the more it hungers for its own perfection, and one perfects itself with the other because of the harmony of their properties with their "fifth instrument" <note>the quintessence</note>, which shares in the celestial cause. For if it did come from Him, the thing would be made by the Creator and not by a creature; thus it would be perfect without destruction. Likewise, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer</note> says in the *Almagest* <note>The influential astronomical manual of the Middle Ages</note>: That the sun does not warm the earth, nor does it impress its power upon the earth, except by the mediation of the moon, which among other stars is more receptive to the light and heat of the sun, acting as a medium between the sun and the earth. Wherefore, as the philosophers say, there are two impediments why one thing does not impress its power upon another: namely, remote distance and an intervening medium. And so it is there between the sun and the earth, because the sun is distant far from the earth, and because the moon mediates there. So also in our alchemical art, the sun <note>representing Gold</note> does not perfect the tincture alone except by the mediation of the moon <note>representing Silver</note>, because it is remotely distant, since it has not yet reached that subtlety required to tinge. Wherefore the moon is necessarily required there, so that she may make the sun itself subtle, rare, and volatile, and segregate its impurity. It must be led back over the earth once more, so that if any of the spirit remains with the earth, that said spirit may be sublimated through the sublimation of the fire of the third degree. It shall then be converted into the foliated earth <term>terra foliata; a flaky, purified state of matter</term> which is called the quintessence <term>quinta essentia; the "fifth element" or purest essence</term> of the earth of metals. By some philosophers, it is called living silver, or Mercury, or the sulphur of nature. And the earth then remaining below, or the powder, is called the dregs and slag—the "condemned powder" which you do not need, for it is a despised powder that vanishes with a modest breath of air. Nevertheless, the overflowing living silver is the earth of the body, passing through the alembic <note>a chemical still used for distillation</note> together with the menstruum <term>a solvent used to extract essences</term>. The sulphur of nature is the sublimated spirit of metals, converted into the foliated earth, which is the first and most immediate matter of metals. This first matter is also called the foliated earth. Moreover, it is necessary that the overflowing spirit be converted into foliated earth through sublimation, so that the pure may be separated from the impure, and the subtle from the thick or coarse terrestrial matter; and so that the vivifying spirit may be drawn out, just as the gaze of the basilisk <note>a mythical serpent whose glance was thought to be a powerful, penetrating force</note> acts upon animals, or as sulphur acts in the melting of metals.

# THE CLANGOR

<margin>The seed of nature and art.</margin>
Metals are generated; for just as metals were generated by nature from the specific seed <note>original: "spermate"</note> of metals, so can they be generated from that same seed most powerfully through Art. Because the quicksilver <term>argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the alchemical name for mercury</term> of the perfect bodies is fixed, since it has been cooked by sulfurous heat in the belly of the earth by a moderate or temperate action. Indeed, the fixed sulfurous quality and the fixed quicksilver quality, deep within the substance of gold and silver, are a fixed substance. And such a substance is most subtle and pure, of the easiest and thinnest liquefaction in the manner of wax, and it is fixed against the struggle of the fire. Therefore, through the said sulfur and through the said quicksilver, they coagulate the quicksilver and convert it into a sun-making <note>original: "solificam," referring to the production of gold</note> and moon-making <note>original: "lunificam," referring to the production of silver</note> nature; they even convert all metallic and imperfect bodies to a perfect nature, both sun-making and moon-making. Therefore, from the aforementioned things, Art works so that this science [achieves] in a few days or hours what nature does in a thousand years.

It is necessary that such a spirit be sealed away in a well-stopped flask; this is according to the intention of Albertus <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a friar and bishop often cited as a primary authority in medieval alchemy.</note>. The other preparing spirit is a moist vapor, not oily but viscous, of the greatest acidity and moderate subtlety. It easily flees the harshness of the fire and vanishes within it, yet it possesses the power of dissolving both bodies and spirits, being a water existing within itself. This is also the view of Albertus and many others, though they describe it under different names. Such a spirit is also called Mercury by an equivocal name, used as a comparison or a metaphorical expression. # THE BLAST

Regarding the elements, this is not to be understood through the literal sense—that it is simply earth, or that it is water, or air, or fire—but rather it is only one single nature, which contains within itself the nature and properties of all the elements.

Likewise, the entire <term>Mastery</term><note>The "Mastery" or Magisterium refers to the complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> consists of this: to divide the elements from the metals, to purify them, and to separate the <term>sulfur of nature</term><note>In alchemy, "sulfur" often represents the active, combustible, or "soul" principle of a substance, rather than common brimstone.</note> from the metals. For the entire labor lies in this, and the whole exhaustion of the Mastery is found in the division of the elements and the sulfur. Thus says Raymond <note>Likely referring to Raymond Lully, a famous 13th-century polymath and purported alchemist.</note>. 

But where he says, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the hermetic tradition.</note> says: "It is necessary for you to extract the four elements," this truly is nothing other than to awaken the <term>seminal virtues</term> themselves—that is, the active or passive qualities. For many who interpret this naturally have fallen into infinite errors. And we say that our spiritual virtue is mineral, which can be intensified and strengthened so that the power of budding and germinating may be introduced. 

And when wishing to receive the mineral elements, do not take from the first nor from the last, but from the middle things for the creation of the <term>Stone</term>, because the first are too simple and the last are too coarse. When you wish to eat, take the bread and leave the flour; and when you wish to make bread, take the flour and leave the wheat. This is our word and the philosophical doctrine; thus says Raymond.

Once the process of dissolving and congealing this earth of ours has been completed, this earth will remain fixed and shining, black when broken, and when projected upon bodies <note>The act of "projection" involves casting the alchemical powder onto molten base metals to transform them</note>, it alters them in their color, but does not yet transform Mercury <note>original: "non Mercuriũ"</note>. Likewise, note concerning the ferment: Nothing is made from that which is already perfect, because it is already perfected, just as this material or art completes it. We have an example: Bread that is fermented and baked is perfect in its state or being, and has reached its ultimate end; you cannot do more with it

For Mercury is not sublimated except through an airy smokiness, carrying with it the purer parts of the body. Therefore, the earth is then converted into air and the body into spirit; density is converted into rarity, and finally they ascend in the manner of air. Thus, by reason of truth, they receive a strong power of penetrating into the depths, and by reason of perfect clarification, they receive the power of perfect tinting and coloration. Therefore, see diligently that the vessels are well joined, because if the Mercury finds an open place, it flies away as smoke; thus the operation will perish and be annihilated, and your <term>mastery</term> <note>the "magisterium" or the completed alchemical goal</note> will be in vain.

### *The Method of Fixing.*

Prepare the ferment—that is, the body before fermentation—so that it may be dissolved and calcined <note>term: calcinatum (calcined) — reduced to a powder through high heat</note>; that is, let the body be dissolved and calcined by means of quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, which means the quicksilver is to be separated and removed from it, and it becomes a most pure lime or ash: for if you have not prepared the ferment, it will be worth nothing. And likewise, prepare the non-burning sulfur <note>term: sulphur non vrens — a philosophical sulfur that represents the active, masculine principle and does not consume the metal in fire</note> from the lime through sublimation <note>term: sublimatio — the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, used here to purify the sulfur</note>, so that it may be simple and "living." For if you do not mix it into the elixir <note>term: elixir — the medicinal or transformative substance capable of transmuting metals</note>, the body upon which the projection of sulfur is made will not be colored. And if you do not cleanse the body which you wish to be mixed into the elixir, the body will not direct the spirit, nor will it retain it. And if you do not sublime this kind of sulfur which you wish to put into the elixir, the gold and silver will be very dark.

Otherwise, the bond of the betrothal would be turned into the flight of the non-fixed spirit and the volatile sulfur. The volatile must not overcome the total amount of the fixed substance united with it.

Hence **Plato** <note>Likely referring to the "Pseudo-Plato" of alchemical tradition rather than the Greek philosopher</note> says: If a little sulfur is cast upon a multitude of the body, so that it has power over it, it converts it into a powder, the color of which will be like the color of the body upon which the spirit of gold or silver is cast. Therefore, in that arrangement:
1. First, you should place the **calx** <term>The powdered remains of a metal after heating; a "corpse" ready for renewal</term> of the body or the ferment.
2. Second, you should place the water, that is, the spirit.
3. Third, you should place the air, that is, the soul, or the sulfur extracted from the bodies.

And to use philosophical eloquence and doctrine: If you first mix oil into earth, the oil will be mortified in the earth, because the oil enters the earth and is swallowed by it. If, however, you first place the water and afterwards the oil, the oil will stand above the water; or if you first place the water and afterwards the earth, the water will be heavier than the earth. Therefore, when you join the elements—namely water and air—so that they may be fixed in the earth: if it is for the **white elixir** <note>The stage of the Great Work that transmutes base metals into silver</note>, there is always more of the earth than of any of the other elements. Otherwise, the earth would not fix the spirit; rather, the spirit would fly away with it. And this ought to be done according to reason, following the measure of equalization...

For example: regarding the lunar elixir <note>The "lunar elixir" refers to the alchemical preparation used to transmute metals into silver.</note>. If there is one and a half parts of air, there ought to be two parts of water, and there ought to be three parts of earth; and let the ferment of the earth be three times as much as the white sulfur <note>original: "sulphur album"; in alchemy, white sulfur represents the purified active principle used for the silver-making process.</note>. So, if there were another half-part of white sulfur, there ought to be three parts of ferment and two of water, and the elixir will be complete. And therefore, keep this precaution in the composition of the true elixir, and work exactly as has been said, so that you know how much you ought to apply of earth, how much of water, and how much of air for the white elixir, and how much of fire for the red <note>The "red elixir" is the final stage of the Great Work, used for transmuting metals into gold.</note>. The reason is that if more of the earth were applied than what was stated, it would kill the soul <note>original: "mortificaret animam"; the 'soul' refers to the volatile, life-giving principle of the substance.</note>. If, however, there were less, the elixir would become too moist and would not be fixed <note>To "fix" a substance means to make it resistant to heat so that it no longer evaporates.</note>. And similarly regarding the water: if more were applied, it would be moist and too soft; if less, it would be dry and hard, and it would not penetrate. And if, similarly, less of the air were applied, it would not color with a perfect color; and if more, it would be perfectly colored in the white elixir.

But for the solar elixir <note>The "solar elixir" is the gold-making medicine.</note>, since the sun is hotter than the moon, there ought to be two parts of earth, three of air, three of water, and one and a half parts of fire; for the weight of the fire is half the weight of the water, and in this there is neither addition nor subtraction.

And if you see that those substances cannot be melted except with difficulty—namely, through a lack of "waxing" <note>original: "incerationis." Inceration is the process of softening a harsh or dry substance until it has a waxy consistency.</note>—
<margin>The sign of true fixation and the final completion.</margin>
supply what is missing, and complete the waxing for it with the "oil of the stone," adding it drop by drop over a light fire in an earthen crucible, until it flows like wax without smoke. Thus says Raymond <note>Referring to Raymond Lull, a famous 13th-century polymath and reputed alchemist.</note>.

<margin>Multiplication of the Stone</margin>
### *On the multiplication or augmentation of the stone.*

Note first what augmentation is. Augmentation is the addition to a pre-existing quantity; and augmentation in quality and goodness is to dissolve and congeal the tincture itself—that is, to soak it in our Mercury and dry it out.

Or do it this way: take one part of the prepared tincture and dissolve it in three parts of our Mercury <note>In alchemy, "our Mercury" usually refers to a purified or philosophical mercury, not common quicksilver.</note>; then place it in a vessel, seal the vessel, and place it among hot ashes throughout the whole process, as expressed above, until it is dried out and becomes a powder. Then open the glass, and soak it again, and dry it as before; and the more often you do this, the more parts you will gain, and the further it will tint <note>The "tincture" is the substance's power to transform base metals into gold; "tinging" refers to this transformative coloring.</note>, as Arnold <note>Referring to Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note> says.

You shall continue these repetitions of the quicksilver powder upon other quicksilver until the quicksilver is no longer converted into powder, but remains converted into perfect metal. This occurs because the strength of the medicine is tempered by the addition of the quicksilver.

Likewise, the multiplication of the tincture is nothing other than the increase and multiplication of the natural heat, which is the **non-burning sulfur** <note>A theoretical alchemical principle representing the active, masculine force that does not consume the substance.</note> within the matter of the quicksilver; for it is certain that quicksilver is the matter of metals in its substance, in which its brightness is fixed.

# HERE BEGINS
## THE PATH OF PATHS.

->*brings forth the vegetable stone <note>The "vegetable stone" in alchemy refers to a substance derived from organic matter, believed to possess life-giving or transformative properties, distinct from the mineral stone.</note>*<-

<margin>The cause of the difference between metals.</margin>
<margin>The sign of the mineral stone.</margin>
Reverend father, incline your pious ears, and understand that Mercury is the seed of all metals, cooked and imperfect in the belly of the earth by sulfurous heat; and according to the sulfurous variety of that heat, diverse metals are generated in the earth. And thus their primordial matter <note>original: "primordialis materia"</note> is one, and naturally, by a greater or lesser action—either burning or not burning—it operates in different ways, and in this all the philosophers <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemists.</note> agree. And I shall demonstrate it in this way: Because it is certain that every thing is made of and from that into which it can be dissolved, and this is a true and similar example. If ice is changed into water by means of heat, therefore, it was previously water: But all metals are converted into Mercury, therefore this Mercury is the first matter <term>First Matter: The formless, original substance from which all things are created.</term>.

<summary>This page introduces the alchemical treatise "The Path of Paths," establishing Mercury as the universal "first matter" from which all metals are formed through varying degrees of sulfurous heat.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury, sulfur, first matter, vegetable stone, alchemy, transmutation of metals, primordial matter</keywords>

# THE PATH

<margin>The first matter of metals,</margin>
their primary substance. I will teach the method of converting them below. Once this is understood, the opinion of those who say that the species of metals cannot be changed is resolved; and this is true, as they say, unless they are first reduced into their "first matter" <note>materia prima: the formless, original substance from which all things are made</note>. However, the reduction of these metals into their first matter is easy, as I shall show. And thus, transmutation is both easy and possible. For everything that grows or is born multiplies within its own species, such as humans, trees, grains, and the like. For from a single grain, a thousand are generated. Therefore, it is possible for things to be increased even unto infinity. From the aforementioned, it appears to the subtle observer that the philosophers in their books spoke obscurely but truly. For they said that our Stone <note>lapis noster: the Philosopher's Stone</note> is composed of body, soul, and spirit, and they speak the truth. For they compared the imperfect body to a "body" because it is weak; and they called the water "spirit," and truly it is spirit, because it grants life to the imperfect body—which is dead by itself—which it did not have before, and brings it forth into a better form. They called the ferment the "soul" because, as will be said below, it similarly grants life to the imperfect body and raises and converts it into its own nature. The Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: "convert the natures, and you will find what you seek," and this is true. For in our mastery <note>magisterio: the alchemical process or "Great Work"</note> we first make the thick thin—that is, we make a spirit from a body—and afterwards we make the moist dry—that is, earth from water—and thus we convert the natures, and we make the above as the below.

This occurs when the spirit is made into a body, and <margin>one vessel</margin> conversely the body is made into a spirit. Likewise, our stone, which is "our water," as the philosophers say, is made from one thing and in one vessel, as they tell you. For the entire <term>mastery<note>original: magisterium; the complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note></term> is done with our water and from it. For it dissolves the bodies as has been said, yet not by that kind of dissolution believed by the ignorant—namely, that it is turned into common rainwater. It also calcines those same bodies and reduces them into earth. It transforms those same bodies into ash, incinerates them, whitens them, and cleanses them according to the word of Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit</note>, who says: That <term>azoth<note>a universal solvent, often identified with mercury</note></term> and fire cleanse the <term>Laton<note>an impure metal or "base" state of the matter</note></term>; that is, they wash it and utterly snatch away its darkness from it. For Laton is the impure body, and azoth is the <term>quicksilver<note>original: argentum vivum; mercury</note></term>. And it joins the diverse bodies, prepared in the manner aforesaid, with such a union that neither fire nor any action can separate them from the burning of the fire; and by one of them rushing into the other, <margin>Against common sublimation.</margin> the change refines the bodies. This is not the common refinement believed by idiots or the inexperienced, who think that to "sublimate" means to ascend upward. Therefore, they take calcined bodies and mix them with sublimated spirits—namely, with Mercury, arsenic, and sulfur, etc.—and they cause them to sublimate by a strong fire (that is, they make the bodies rise with the spirits) and they say that the bodies are then "sublimated." But they are deluded, because they still find the bodies to be more impure with the spirits than they were before. Therefore, our "sublimating" is not ascending upward, but rather...

# THE PATHWAY

<margin>Philosophical sublimation.</margin> To refine, in the manner of the philosophers, is to take a thing most vile and corrupted (from the earth) and make from it another more pure. Just as we say a man is "sublimated" into a bishop—meaning he is exalted or placed in a more worthy state—so too do we say that bodies are converted or exalted into another, better nature. Thus, to sublimate is the same as to make subtle <note>To "subtilize" or refine a solid into a more spiritual or gaseous state</note>, all of which is accomplished by our water. This is how philosophical sublimation is to be understood, a point on which many have been deceived. <margin>The effects of the water.</margin> Our water also mortifies <note>original: "mortificat"; refers to the "death" or breakdown of the initial material</note>, illuminates, cleanses, and brings to life. It causes black colors to appear first during the mortification of the body while it is being turned into earth; afterwards, many and varied colors appear before the whitening. <margin>The first blackness.</margin> The end of all these colors is whiteness. Indeed, in the mixing of the water and the body of the leaven <note>original: "fermenti"; the substance that triggers the transformation</note>—that is, the prepared body—infinite colors appear. Thus it is evident that our mastery <term>Magisterium: the complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> is from one thing, and is done with one thing; it is from four, and from three, it becomes one.

Wherefore you should know, Father, that the philosophers have multiplied the names of the "mixed stone," and they have done this so that they might hide it. They called it a mixed stone, both corporeal and spiritual, and they did not lie, as a wise man is able to understand. For there is both body and spirit; the body is only spiritual during the solution <note>The stage where solids are dissolved into liquid</note>, and it is made into spirit; and it is corporeal during the conjunction of the spirit with the body. And the leaven...

# THE PATHS

Allow it to cool for a natural day <note>A "natural day" refers to a full 24-hour cycle.</note>, and when you find it has cooled, strain the water along with everything inside it through a linen cloth, until that which has been dissolved from the body passes through the cloth. The part, however, which is unable to pass through should be set aside.

Then take that which remained in the cloth and place it back on the fire with new blessed water <note>original: "aqua benedicta"; in alchemy, this usually refers to a purified solvent or acidified water rather than a religious substance</note> in the aforementioned vessel for a natural day; afterwards, strain it as before. Repeat this process as many times as necessary until the entire body is converted into water—that is, into the first matter <note>original: "prima materia"; the formless primordial substance from which all elements arise</note>, which is our water. When this is done, place all that water into a glass vessel and cook it over a slow fire until you see blackness appear on its surface. Remove this blackness carefully by collecting it daily, until the entire body is dissolved into pure earth. Do this as many times and as well as you can, cooking it again and removing the blackness until no more blackness appears and the water—that is, the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; literally "living silver" or mercury</note>—appears clear. Then you possess the water and the earth.

Next, take all of this earth—that is, the blackness which you collected—and place it in a glass vessel. Pour the aforementioned blessed water over it until nothing sticks out and the water floats above it. Cook it thus with a light fire for ten days; grind it, and again add water and cook it.

And so on in succession: that is, you shall cook the earth, thus coagulated and thickened with water, over a strong fire as described above, without adding any further water, until the earth becomes white and clear. Once it has been purified and whitened as stated, and the water of life <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; here referring to a potent distilled solvent or spirit</note> which was thickened by means of gentle heat with the said coagulated earth, you must cook it with a strong fire in a sturdy gourd-shaped vessel <note>original: "cucurbita"</note> with a still-head <note>original: "alembico"</note> placed on top, until whatever water was therein descends through the still-head, and the earth remains calcined <note>reduced to a powder by heat</note>. 

Then take a fourth part of any ferment; for example, if there was a pound of the imperfect body (that is, of lesser value), you should take three pounds of the ferment, namely of the sun <note>gold</note> or the moon <note>silver</note>. And let that ferment be dissolved and turned into earth, just like the imperfect body, and prepared in the same manner and order. Join them together and soak them with the aforementioned blessed water <note>original: "aqua benedicta"; likely the distilled spirit collected earlier</note>, that is, with the water which ascended the still-head. 

Cook this for three days or more, then soak it again with its own water and cook as before. Repeat this as many times as necessary until these two bodies remain as one—that is, they are reduced into one substance. You will judge this to be done when the color among them no longer varies. Then, by pouring the aforementioned water over them by itself little by little, continue until it has drunk as much as it can possibly drink, always giving them fresh water. For in this joining of the bodies, the spirit is mixed with them and becomes one with them, and it is converted into their nature, the aforementioned bodies having been purified. ### _Recapitulatio of all things_
### _previously stated._

Now I shall return, Reverend Father, to the things said previously, applying them specifically to the perfections of the ancient philosophers and their obscure, unbearable, and hidden words. If you truly judge the words of the Philosophers, you will understand, and thus you may affirm that they have brought forth your own words.

<margin>Note the body of water.</margin>
The first word of our mastery or work is the reduction of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury</note> (of the body), that is, the reduction of copper or another metal into quicksilver. And this is what the philosophers call "solution" <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</note>, which is the foundation of the art, as Franciscus <note>likely referring to Cecco d'Ascoli or another medieval authority</note> says: "Unless you dissolve the bodies, you labor in vain." Parmenides speaks of this solution in the *Assembly* <note>original: "in turma"; referring to the 'Turba Philosophorum,' one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>. Hearing of this solution, the ignorant think it is "water of the clouds" <note>rainwater</note>. If, however, they had read and understood our books, they would certainly know that it is "permanent water" <note>a fixed, non-volatile liquid</note>, which, when joined with its body, is made into one permanent thing. Therefore, the solution of the philosophers is not rainwater, but the conversion of bodies into liquid water.

# THE PATH

<margin>The seed of metals.</margin>
...chosen, so that you may weigh in your mind what I am about to say. For the elements are not generated except from their own specific seed. This seed is "living silver" <note>original: "argentum viuum," commonly known as quicksilver or mercury</note>, just as is evident in the generation of a human being; for there is no mingling of any thing except through the seed, nor in plants except through the seed, as far as their generation and growth are concerned. Others, looking more subtly into the matter, sublime the Mercury <note>A process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then becomes solid again</note>, and fix it, and join it with the bodies of metals, and yet they find nothing. The cause of their error is this: for the seed cannot be changed from what it is or was, nor is it useful unless it be cast into the womb of a woman. Thus the Philosopher Mechardus <note>Likely a corruption of a name like Richardus or a specific Arabic authority cited in medieval alchemy</note> says: Unless the stone is cast into the womb of the woman so that she may nourish it, it is of no use. O my father, thus you have according to your desire the description of the philosophers' stone.

Praise be to God.

# THE LITTLE
## TREATISE OF AVI-
### CENNA.

->*I shall divide this book into eight chapters or*<-
->*parts.*<-

In the first chapter, I shall speak of Mercury <note>The "spirit" or liquid principle in alchemy</note> and its nature, as well as the sulfur which it contains within itself.
In the second, I shall speak of the nature of the perfect bodies <note>Gold and silver</note> and their sulfur.
In the third, I shall speak of the joining of the body and the spirit, and the dissolution of the stone into its first matter.
In the fourth, I shall speak of the extraction of the water from the earth.
In the fifth, I shall speak of the foundation or the pouring [of the water] upon its own earth.
In the sixth, I shall speak of the method of the sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and solidifies again</note> of the earth.
In the seventh, I shall speak of the multiplication and the fixing of the stone.
In the eighth and final chapter, I shall speak of the method of projecting the medicine <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or elixir</note> and of tinting any metal into the Sun and the Moon <note>Gold and silver</note>.

# A LITTLE TREATISE

## Chapter I.

<margin>This matches the copy in the *Theatrum Chemicum* <note>original: "Th. chim."</note> regarding the white action in some <unclear>g</unclear> parts.</margin>

Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum viuum"</note> is cold and moist, and God created all minerals from it or with it. It is of the nature of air and flees from fire, but when it has remained in the fire for a little while, it performs wonderful <gloss>high</gloss> and strange works.

## *dissolution of the stone into the first matter.*

It is certain that every thing is made of that into which it is dissolved. For ice is converted into water by means of heat. It is clear, therefore, that it was water before it was ice. Truly, all metals are generated from Mercury; therefore, they are resolved back into it.

# AVICENNA

The first treatment <term>regimen; the controlled process of alchemical transformation</term> of the stone, therefore, is to dissolve it, just like thick quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note>, so that it may be reduced into its first matter. This entire process is achieved through quicksilver, because it has the power to reduce the sun <note>gold</note> and the moon <note>silver</note> into their own nature and first matter. 

But since quicksilver contains within itself dross and a capacity for scorching without flame, as well as a watery substance, it is therefore necessary to remove its superfluities and fulfill what is lacking if you wish to make a complete medicine <note>the Elixir or Stone</note> from it. It is absolutely necessary to remove the drossy earth by means of sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collects as a solid again to purify it</note>, and to fulfill what is lacking, lest it create a leaden color during the projection <note>the final stage of alchemy where the medicine is cast upon base metals to transform them</note>. In the same way, one must destroy its wateriness, lest it make the entire material fly away <note>evaporate or become volatile</note> during projection.

It is the property of this [purified] substance to preserve the essence of the medicine, to remain unburned, but rather to fix <note>to make a volatile substance stable under heat</note> the matter and defend it from scorching. For this reason, it happens that Saturn <note>lead</note>, Jupiter <note>tin</note>, Venus <note>copper</note>, iron, etc., are created from it, which necessarily occurs because of impurity.

**It is to be noted:** That the "first matter" is twofold. One is "proximate" <note>immediate</note>, while the other is "remote." The proximate matter is quicksilver; the remote matter is water, because quicksilver was first water, and afterwards became quicksilver. Therefore, the true beginning of our work is the dissolution of the stone, because dissolved bodies are reduced to the nature of a spirit, because they are more fixed.

### *On the multiplication and fixation of the stone.*
## Chapter VII.

Truly, in the decoction <note>The process of heating or boiling.</note> after the whiteness, you cannot err. For as the governance of the fire is gradually increased, one arrives after the whiteness at the yellowing, and then at the red.

Note, let the regimen of fire be governed according to nature and by the example of the four seasons. In the first season, namely winter, the earth conceives. # AVICENNA

<margin><unclear>...</unclear></margin>
Regarding the promise I have fulfilled up to this point, the great mastery <note>Latin: magisterium magnum; the complete process of alchemical transformation</note> for making the most excellent white and red elixir. Here, finally, I shall speak of the method of projection <note>The act of casting the alchemical powder onto molten base metal to transform it</note>, which is the completion of the work, and the joy so desired and expected. The White Elixir indeed whitens unto infinity, and it brings whatever metal it touches to perfect whiteness <note>Transformation into silver</note>. But it must be known that one metal is brought to the elixir more easily than another. For those things which are near to perfection are transformed more perfectly than those which are remote. And when we find a metal that is perfect and very near, the vice of imperfection is excused in that near thing by those things which are far remote; which metals are far remote or near is made clear enough in many books.

And because the white or red elixir is highly spiritual, yet works beyond the laws of nature, it is no wonder that it is able to be mixed with the body upon which it is projected, provided that it merely liquefies that body.

<margin>A Caution for the Eggs <note>Likely a metaphorical term for the alchemical vessels or the starting material</note></margin>
It is a heavy task to project upon a thousand times a thousand parts and have it penetrate them immediately. Therefore, I shall hand down to you one great secret. One part is to be mixed with a thousand parts of a closely related body <note>A base metal similar in property to the desired result</note>, and shut all of this firmly in a suitable vessel; it must be placed in a melting furnace for three days, until the whole has been inseparably joined together.

And that is the "work of three days"; then, one part of that body may be projected unto infinity.

### Concerning the seed of metals, the material of the stone.

By this it is demonstrated to you that first you must dissolve the bodies in our solvent <note>original: "menstruo"; a specialized alchemical liquid used to break down solid metals</note>, then you must divide the elements from the luminaries <note>The "luminaries" refer to the Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver)</note>, and purify and fix those elements, and extract the sulfur of nature from the perfected bodies.

Thirdly, you must unite elements with elements, or "slime" with "slime," or the elements with the sulfur of nature. And this union is divided into as many parts as there are mixtures and unions of the aforementioned things.

The first mode is to unite **air** with **fire**.

The second mode is to unite **air** with the **sulfur of nature**, and these modes exist within the elements of the two luminary bodies <insert>Gold and Silver</insert>.

The third mode is to unite the slime arising from air in fire, with the slime arising from air and the sulfur of nature, solely by itself. The fourth mode is that fire be united by itself, and air by itself, with the sulfur of nature only. The fifth mode is to mix the sulfur of nature with two elements at once, namely with fire and air. And these modes of mixing the elements with the sulfur of nature occur in two ways: for they are done either with their own earth or with a foreign earth. Indeed, with foreign earth it is done in as many multiple ways as there are modes of mixing the sulfur of nature, according to the pleasure of the artist. # OF TRANSMUTATION

Any <term>putrefaction</term><note>The process of breaking down a substance through gentle heat to separate its components</note> requires eight days, or six continuous ones, such that the division of the elements lasts nearly a year. Furthermore, there are some who, when they cannot divide their elements and the <term>sulfur of nature</term><note>In alchemy, 'sulfur' represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of a substance</note> as quickly as they desire, refuse to pay attention to the natures of the minerals. They create a confused mixture without any purification, sublimation, or refinement. Thus, they do not reach the sought-after end, attributing no cause to their own ignorance, but instead laying the blame upon the Art which they do not understand. They assert that the Art is false; we believe you, O King, to be one of their number. Therefore, do not grow weary, nor cease from the work, and you shall find what you desire. For you must know, O King, how to combine the natural principles, and that which you seek shall come to pass.

# HERE BEGINS
## THE BOOK CALLED THE LADDER OF PHILOSOPHERS.

<insert>118</insert>
<margin>The first physical division.</margin>
<margin>The cause of natural love.</margin>
As the Venerable Raymond Lully <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan philosopher and mystic to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note> says: The intention of nature for performing our mastery <note>The "mastery" or "magistery" refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is that the stone <term>lapis: the primary material of the alchemical work</term> must be divided into the four elements, so that each one by itself, according to the requirements of nature, can be purified. And that is the preparation of things which precedes the operation of perfect preparation; it is properly called the "separation of the elements," because it divides all the impure parts from the pure parts. This is done so that, with the lighter and purer parts, our perfect preparation may be achieved successively through a natural joining. This joining is performed by the reduction of the moist with the dry, immediately after they have been prepared through the benefit of the separation of elements. Otherwise, the moist would not "love" the dry, nor the body the spirit, if they were not first well-washed of their infections by means of distillations, calcinations <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or achieve oxidation.</note>, solutions, and coagulations. For through the separation of the elements, the falsehood of its burning sulfurousness is burned away—a quality which came to it through the original stain of our menstrual water <note>original: "menstrualis"; in alchemy, this refers to the "solvent" or the base "mother" material that requires purification from its raw, "bloody" state.</note>, which

It emphasizes that the "natural love" or chemical affinity between substances can only occur once they are cleansed of their original impurities.</summary>
<keywords>Raymond Lully, Ladder of Philosophers, separation of elements, purification, sulfurousness, alchemy, four elements, calcination</keywords>

# THE LADDER

It must be known that there are four principal regimes <term>regimina: the stages or methods of treatment</term> of our stone: namely, dissolving, washing, joining, and fixing.

<margin>The diverse methods of those who labor.</margin>
The operation of the <term>stone</term><note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> is described in many ways by the philosophers. For some rectify the parts individually, then compose them, and afterwards bring them to perfection. This operation is varied in many ways; it is laborious, difficult, and subtle. Therefore, many err in it, because the support—that is, the assistance—of that work requires many external things. Nevertheless, the operation of this stone is one, following a single line, and it is perfected in one single vessel. The fire, however, is not uniform throughout the entire action. And so, in order that this treatise may suffice and be of benefit to students, I say that the internal fire of this work is like the heat of the sun in the <term>greater world</term><note>The "macrocosm" or the universe at large, as opposed to the "microcosm" of the alchemical vessel.</note>. Indeed, in the springtime, the sun is moderate and light in its heat. Otherwise, the plants, which are tender, would be withered and would bear no fruit at all. This heat enters the plants until they grow little by little; and the more they grow, the more the heat of the sun gradually grows or increases daily, until the crops are whitened. When spring is finished, summer begins; and because the sun is then stronger, it becomes strongest until the end of <term>Leo</term><note>The zodiac sign of the Lion, associated with the height of summer and the most intense heat.</note>, until all things receive their due form and perfection. And blessed be God, who has wonderfully ordained these things by His wisdom. In a similar way, therefore, this stone must be ruled. For some say that the heat of the first <term>regimen</term><note>A specific stage or method of controlling the alchemical fire.</note> ought to be like that of a hen sitting upon her eggs to produce chicks. Others, however, say that it ought to be like the natural heat that digests food and nourishes the body.

<margin>The Sun in Aries, etc.</margin>

Others, like the heat of the sun when it is in Aries <note>The sign of the Ram, marking the spring equinox</note>, because the sun has its dominion and exaltation there, for there it begins to rise and grow warm in a moderate degree.

And for this reason, some have said that we ought to begin while the sun is in Aries and the moon is staying in Taurus <note>The sign of the Bull</note>: all of which things were said to designate a moderate heat regarding the first action of this work. And although the action of this stone is a single one—namely, decoction <term>decoction: a process of boiling or heating to extract essence</term> with natural fire—nevertheless, the state of this heat is varied in a threefold way. First, there will be a moderate fire, and it lasts until the blackness <note>original: "nigredinem"; the first stage of the Great Work, representing decomposition</note> appears, and even until that blackness is converted into whiteness <note>original: "albedinem"; the second stage, representing purification</note>.

<margin>The time of blackness</margin>
This blackness lasts perhaps forty-six days, or more or less, according to the diligence of the operator and the guidance of fortune; and this heat is likened to the heat of the sun passing from Aries into Taurus. When a certain whiteness appears, let the fire be increased step by step, until the perfect drying or incineration <term>incineration: reducing a substance to ashes</term> of the stone, and this heat is likened to the heat of the sun in Taurus, traveling into Gemini <note>The sign of the Twins</note>.

Indeed, once the stone is dried and incinerated, the fire is strengthened again until the stone becomes most perfectly red, and is clothed by the fire in a royal garment.

And this heat is likened to the heat of the sun in Leo <note>The sign of the Lion</note>, for this is the house of its own dignity. Then let it be continued until it becomes a poison <note>In alchemy, "venenum" or poison often refers to a potent, transformative substance or the "penetrating" quality of the elixir</note>.

But here it must be understood that every alteration of minerals toward their perfection stands in the higher rank of spiritual things. We are not speaking here of angels, nor of heavenly intelligences, but of the higher degree of perfection found in all metals, and this resides in the mineral spirit. For minerals agree with minerals, and vegetables with vegetables, so that there is no opposition between them, but rather the greatest harmony. This is because this spirit is of a golden mineral nature, and does not differ from gold except in this: that gold is fixed <note>Stable and resistant to fire.</note>, while the spirit is not fixed.

Thus, our gold is not the common gold of the masses, because ours is spiritual. It dissolves all imperfect bodies, separating the pure from the impure, since nature receives only what belongs to its own nature and rejects what is foreign—which is the very sign of its perfection. Therefore, it dissolves, separates, divides, purifies, and illuminates all bodies; it dyes them and transmutes them into the finest gold, because it is a fixed body made spiritual, and according to the various stages of digestion <note>original: "diges", catchword for the following page.</note>

To congeal the spirit is our primary work, because the body is not dissolved unless the spirit is congealed. Nor is the spirit congealed except through the dissolution of the body. For if they are joined together at the same time, each acts upon the other, just as water acts upon the earth mixed with it; therefore, you must refine it according to its own manner.

For the earth is not refined unless the water is thickened, nor is the water thickened unless the earth is refined. Thus, between the congealing of the spirit and the dissolution of the body, there is no difference in time, nor is the work diverse, because each acts upon the other in its own way. For action and passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression, a standard term in medieval alchemy and philosophy.</note> do not result from things contrary in species but similar in genus and nature; and when one of the contraries exceeds the other, it destroys or alters the remainder. According to this, when the body is mixed with humidity and placed over a slow fire for a long time, it is dissolved, because the humidity turns upon it and dissolves it. Meanwhile, the body—by means of its coldness and dryness—encloses, retains, and thickens the moisture, incinerating that which is dry. And yet, the humidity cannot exit from the body unless it absorbs itself along with the fire.

For when the appropriate heat is at work through the process of putrefaction <note>The stage of "putrefaction" was considered essential in alchemy to break down substances before they could be reborn or transformed.</note>, the moist is turned into the dry. And therefore, when you have dissolved the body, you congeal the moist; and this happens with a delay, which is chiefly due to the four clashing elements, so that peace may be made between them.

<summary>This page describes the alchemical principle of "solve et coagula," explaining the reciprocal relationship between the dissolution of the body and the congealing of the spirit. It emphasizes that these processes occur simultaneously through the balancing of the four elements over a slow heat.</summary>

# T H E  L A D D E R

## The third step of the ladder of the 
## wise.

The four aforementioned conflicting elements, having been distinguished from one another and subsequently rectified through distillation, are separated in this third step of the ladder of the wise. Therefore, this step is called our **Separation**. This is the separation of the watery or liquid vapor from the dregs; it is a purification, a smoothing of the subtle parts, an extraction of the coarse parts, a division of those things joined together, a production of principles, and a segregation of homogeneous parts.
Hence the Psalm: *He brought water out of the rock and oil* <margin>Water bath. Dry heat.</margin> *out of the hardest stone.* <note>A reference to Psalm 81:16 and Deuteronomy 32:13, interpreted here as the extraction of precious essences from base matter.</note> This must be done in appropriate water baths <term>balneum: a vessel placed in hot water for gentle heating</term> and afterwards in dry heat <term>stuffa: a dry oven or stove</term>, according to the requirements of reason. From these substances, their phlegm <note>original: "flegma"; the watery, tasteless distillate</note> is first separated and evacuated in the water baths. Then, those four principles are separated from the beginning according to the required signs—especially the Moon <note>alchemical symbol for Silver or the feminine principle</note>, the male before the female. Thus, with their mother left in the bottom during the first distillation, you shall reserve the lemon-colored sapphire <note>original: "saphiram citrinam"; likely referring to a yellow-tinted distillate</note>. Afterward, the orpiment <term>auripigmentum: arsenic trisulfide, used here as a chemical stage</term> is rectifyingly separated in the dry heat, both from its moisture and by itself, so many times until nothing rises in the southern redness <note>a reference to the "rubedo" or reddening stage of the work</note> and the orpiment remains clear and white. This is perfected in the third or fourth attempt. The signs of its perfection are greenness, whiteness, and purity, without dregs—unless they happen to be white. Its greenness comes from the coldness of the soul...
