# THE LADDER

## The fourth step of our ladder of
## wisdom is, and is called,
## Conjunction.

Therefore, once the four distinct elements have been separated as previously described and rectified, we join and connect those same four together. Our <term>conjunction</term><note>The act of joining separated elements back together into a unified whole.</note> is called a mingling of qualities, a coupling of embracing things, a refolding of scattered parts, an equalization of principles, and an arrangement for the reconciliation of opposites.

For the <term>Rosary</term><note>Refers to the 'Rosarium Philosophorum' (The Rosary of the Philosophers), a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> says: Arrange the airy substance through discernment so that the earth may be obtained from two natures, and the water, as previously stated, from two bodies. In this way, the subtle is separated from the gross, and the thin from the thick. Clearly, what we have described must be done gently and with great ingenuity—that is, with a proper and nourishing heat. For no water is necessary for our work unless it is bright, nor any oil unless it is white and shining with a yellow tint, nor any earth unless it is pale and whitish. For then the earth is fit for binding, the water for dissolving, and the air is overflowing for the purpose of tinting.

And there are two earths and two waters in our work. The first earth, which remains at the bottom during the first distillation, is properly pale; it is upon this that our rectification is performed. Once the oil has been separated from this earth (as was hinted at above, albeit in a confused manner) and similarly from the water, the oil is distilled again by itself; and then that which—

<margin>The Triple Union...</margin>

# THE LADDER

The triple union <note>original: "Triptatiua coniunctio"</note>, that is, the union of the trinity, is made from body, spirit, and soul. For according to the philosophers, just as the soul is the bond of the spirit, so also the body is the bond of the soul; this is because the spirit penetrates, the body fixes <note>In alchemy, "fixing" refers to making a volatile substance solid or stable</note>, and the soul joins them together. Thus, this trinity is a unity in essence, because they are co-eternal and <margin>The Quadruple Union</margin> co-equal.

The quadruple union is called the correction of the principles, so that one of them may be perfected in the other. Therefore, for the most praiseworthy union, it is necessary that the four elements in our work be in a composition that is liquid, fresh, warm, and properly proportioned.

<margin>A marvelous comparison.</margin> Since equality does not arise from three, but from four opposing things prevailing in nature; and just as a woman has fifteen veins and a man has five <note>This refers to medieval anatomical theories regarding the "humors" and reproductive fluids</note>. And you should know that our fiery water is a sharp, menstrual water <note>original: "aqua menstruosa," a term used in alchemy to describe a solvent that acts like a life-giving or transformative fluid</note>. Then, when four parts of the first lime <note>original: "calcis," referring to a powdered mineral or metallic oxide</note> are dissolved within it, and its four congealed natures are applied, everything is suddenly blackened by putrefaction. Therefore, for the first, second, and third soakings <term>imbibition: the process of a solid absorbing a liquid</term>, one must apply in turn 12 parts of fresh water to 4 parts of earth. And always, at each turn, use the ratio of 4 to 2. But on the seventh turn, 2 parts are applied which, when added to the other 2 parts of sharpened water after congealment, perform the third act. With these, as before, the substance is completely blackened, and thereafter it is guided toward perfection through decoction <note>prolonged heating</note> alone without further addition, according to the *Rosary*, whose completion of the process is said to be achieved through sublime means.

Hence Averroes <note>original: "Aurois," referring to the Andalusian philosopher</note> says: To dissolve the body and congeal the spirit is the first work of nature, as was said before.

And it must be known that the soul is the bond of the spirit, just as the body is the bond of the soul. When you are engaged in the work, let there be persistence and patience with appropriate expectation, the end of which is profit and joy; let there also be no laziness, negligence, or "devilish haste," the end of which is loss and sadness.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical processes, specifically focusing on the refinement of the "Stone" through sublimation and exaltation.</meta>

# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

For the methods of our sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again to purify it.</note> and exaltation <note>A process intended to raise a substance to a higher state of "nobility" or potency.</note> do not differ in essence, except that by this sublimation alone is understood the enabling of the stone, and the perfect joining of the ferment <note>The agent that triggers transformation, similar to yeast in bread.</note> with it. At that time also, the medicine is simple but not yet perfect, nor is it at its most perfect until the medicine is made noble through exaltation and raised up, as appears below. And it should be known that we perform sublimation for four reasons.

First, so that the body may become a spirit of subtle matter.
Second, so that Mercury <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity and volatility.</note> may incorporate itself with the body and become one with it.
Third, so that the whole may become white, and then red, and clean, and so that the saltiness of the sulfur <note>Sulfur represents the principle of combustibility and soul.</note> may be diminished, and especially so that the innate moisture of the stone may be restored—which it first lost in the lime <note>original: "calce"; referring to the powdery residue left after heating (calcination).</note>—and that it may be effectively enabled for the quickest liquefaction. 

<margin>What the medicine is.</margin>
For the medicine ought to be a simple powder of the most subtle and pure substance, adhering to quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury.</note> by its own nature, and of the easiest liquefaction, of hidden refinement, and of the thinnest penetration just like water. Furthermore, it must remain fixed against the battle of the fire before the flight of the Mercury; then, whatever is added to it will be of the same temperament as that to which it is added. For instance, if you add water to it, the whole will dissolve into water; but if you place it in the fire, the whole will be of the fire.

# THE LADDER

And this is the reason why our medicine <note>The "medicine" refers to the Philosopher's Stone in its final, curative state for both metals and the human body.</note> must be multiplied infinitely.

For the medicine itself is like fire within wood, and like musk among fine spices. Therefore, it grows the more it is pressed into use; for this reason, you must always leave a portion of it behind, since one who is enriched by it is enriched just as one who possesses fire is enriched by fire <note>Meaning that like a flame, the Stone can kindle new "fires" without losing its own essence.</note>.

<margin>Note</margin>
The medicine can be multiplied in two ways. First, through dissolution and repeated coagulation; this is its multiplication in power <note>original: "virtualis"</note> regarding its quality.

<margin>Increase through fermentation.</margin>
The second way is through fermentation, and this is its multiplication in quantity. You will complete the increase through fermentation more quickly, because the dissolved substance does not work well unless it is first fixed in its own ferment. Therefore, our medicine is multiplied more perfectly through the exaltation of dissolution—and in this way, things become spiritual—and after the first dissolution, exaltation, and coagulation, one part in the first projection <note>The act of casting the medicine onto base metal to transform it.</note> falls upon 100 parts; in the second, upon 1,000; and thus further by tenfold, always by exalting it, even unto infinity, which is the most precious gift of God. Thus it is concluded that it works more abundantly in a great quantity of fermented and dissolved medicine, because the ferment alone is more refined, although it could be multiplied infinitely through fermentation alone—

<term>Medicine: The final alchemical agent or Philosopher's Stone.</term>
<term>Multiplication: The process of increasing the power or quantity of the Stone.</term>
<term>Dissolution: Breaking a solid down into a liquid state.</term>
<term>Coagulation: Returning a liquid to a solid state.</term>
<term>Fermentation: Adding a "leaven" (usually gold or silver) to the Stone to fix its nature.</term>
<term>Exaltation: A process that raises the substance to a higher formal dignity or potency.</term>
<term>Spiritual things: Substances that have been refined into a volatile or non-corporeal state.</term>
<term>Projection: The final step of alchemy where the Stone transforms base metal into gold.</term>

...and this is because a ferment <note>Latin: *fermentum*; in alchemy, a substance that triggers a transformation in another, much like yeast in bread</note> draws whatever is placed near it back to its own natural color and flavor in every possible way. Therefore, when the philosophers saw that the substance did not flee <note>i.e., did not evaporate or escape as vapor</note> when it was made volatile with other volatile things, they returned it to a similar non-volatile body. They brought it into that very thing from which they could least escape, because of the close harmony of its nature. Indeed, the soul enters its own body more quickly than if it were placed in another; if you strive to place it elsewhere, you will labor in vain, because there is no <margin>Mixing</margin> binding together of darkness and light. Therefore, they returned to a body similar to the bodies from which they were drawn, and they were prepared, because in this way the dyer and the thing to be dyed were made into one single dye <note>Latin: *tinctura*; the transformative agent or "elixir" that changes the color and nature of metals</note>. Do not think, therefore, that the substance which dyes and then flees is the true dye of the philosophers. For though <margin>they flee</margin> sulfurs <note>Latin: *sulphura*; representing the active, combustible principle in alchemy</note> may dye and shape things, they do not do so unless they are joined to a similar quicksilver <note>Latin: *argentum vivum*; mercury, representing the fluid or passive principle</note> of their own kind. Therefore, it must be mixed with quicksilver—one white, the other red—of its own kind, lest the dye flee. For this reason, we command that quicksilver be mixed with quicksilver, as was said before, until it becomes one clean water.

And this must be known, Adarnech <note>likely a corruption of Adfar, an alchemical authority, or a specific student addressed in the text</note>, that all the names of things and their similarities are contradicted by the ancients for no other reason than so that you might understand that the beginning of this matter bears witness to the end. And also know that this whole thing is nothing but one single thing, which has a father and a mother; and its father and mother have mixed it and they nourish it.

<summary>This page explains the alchemical principle of "fermentation," where a volatile spirit (soul) is stabilized by being reunited with a compatible solid body to create a permanent dye or tincture. It emphasizes that the work involves unifying similar substances, specifically different forms of quicksilver, into a single "clean water."</summary>

->THE LADDER OF PHILOSOPHY<-

nor can these things differ in any way from their own mother.
Therefore, once the materials are mixed, so that they may be multiplied through fixation <note>original: "confixationem"; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>, place the vessel over the fire and guard the smoke, taking precautions lest any of it escape. The entire governance of the work consists in waiting during the time of the fire; stay near the vessel and observe how the medicine will change from color to color in less than one hour of the day, until it reaches the goal of whiteness <note>original: "albedinis"; the Albedo stage of the alchemical process</note>. For it will liquefy very quickly in the fire and congeal in the air, because the smoke, when it feels the heat, will penetrate the body, and the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; the volatile or gaseous aspect of the matter</note> will be broken down into a dry substance. It will then become a single, fixed, clear body, either white or red, depending on what the medicine and the ferment <note>original: "fermentum"; the catalyst added to the base matter</note> were. Then extinguish the fire and allow the whole to cool, because one part of this weight falls upon a thousand thousand, even twelve hundred thousand parts of any body, so that it may be converted into the finest gold or silver, according to the quality of the elixir.

# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

...to act, now you dismiss <note>original: "nunc dimittis"</note> upon the foundations, and the foundations upon my words, and my words upon "I will love thee, O Lord," and "I will love thee" upon "take heed." <note>The author is using liturgical phrases—likely from the Psalms and the Song of Simeon—as mnemonic devices or spiritual markers for the stages of the alchemical process.</note> An example of this is found in saffron: if it is thrown in while dry, it tints but little; however, if it is dissolved and joined with a small amount of liquid, that small portion can then tint a vast amount infinitely. Thus shall you perform the <term>projection</term> <note>The final stage of alchemy where the "Philosopher's Stone" is cast upon base metal to transform it.</note>: first multiply 10 by 10, which will be 100; then 100 by a thousand, which will be ten thousand, and so on through common numbers unto infinity. Now, the cause of these things is entirely twofold: namely, of goodness, of necessity, and of perfection. Of goodness, so that it may tint more abundantly, perform better, and convert more material. Of necessity, so that it may be better colored, better fixed, and enter into that which is like itself. Of perfection, because the perfect medicine has the power to <margin>con-</margin>vert <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver, often viewed as the "mother" of all metals.</note> into the most perfect gold and silver. Furthermore, the perfect number is the ten, the hundred, and the thousand. Therefore, from the beginning to the last, you shall perform the projection. For if so small an amount were cast into the fire upon so great a mass, it would be endangered by the fire on account of its smallness. Truly, all the foundations of the medicine must be greatly refined and tinged.

# THE LADDER

### *An epilogue of the whole and a summary recapitulation*
### *of all the things mentioned above.*

Therefore, let the stone <note>original: "lapis"; the primary material of the alchemical work</note> be taken, which is sufficiently known from the previous chapters. And with diligent application of the work, let the perfection of sublimation <note>the process of vaporizing and re-condensing a substance to purify it</note> be repeatedly performed upon it, so that by this it may be cleansed and refined, until it reaches the ultimate purity of subtlety, and finally becomes volatile <note>able to be evaporated</note>; this indeed is the first stage of its administration.

From this point, let it be fixed <note>original: "fixionis"; the process of making a volatile substance stable in fire</note> by the methods of fixation, until it rests calmly in the harshness of the fire. In this way, the work of the moon <note>original: "lunæ"; referring to the creation of silver</note> becomes exceedingly white, and the work of the sun <note>original: "solis"; referring to the creation of gold</note> becomes exceedingly red. Because the white work belongs to winter and the red work to summer, it therefore requires a greater refinement of its parts through specific methods in a longer decoction of digestion <note>prolonged heating at a steady temperature</note>, namely until it assumes a most deep red color. And the goal of the second stage of preparation consists in this single perfection.

But the completion of the entire work is found in the third stage: namely, that you make the now-fixed stone volatile again by methods of refinement, and again make the volatile fixed, and the fixed dissolved, and the dissolved once more volatile, and the volatile once more fixed, until it flows and transforms in certain completion, both "sun-making" <note>original: "solifico"; gold-making</note> and "moon-making" <note>original: "lunifico"; silver-making" </note>. For from the repetition of the preparation of this third stage in the medicine <note>the final alchemical elixir</note>, there results a great increase of transformation and of goodness.

<summary>This page provides a three-stage summary of the alchemical Great Work, detailing the transition of the "stone" through sublimation, fixation, and repeated cycles of dissolution to create a transformative elixir.</summary>

# TREATISE
## THE WORK OF WOMEN
### AND WHAT IS CALLED CHILD’S PLAY

->It begins auspiciously.<-

The progression of the Work is called "all the work of women and child’s play." After the beginning of the work, the subtle investigator of divine nature continues the progress. Therefore, these words are not fables, nor are they worthy of contempt; indeed, you should pay such attention to these words that the texts of the ancient books do not deceive you, for they sometimes transpose words, as the philosopher Apuleius <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, a name often attached to medieval botanical and alchemical texts</note> says in his book *On the Secrets of Nature*.

Furthermore, a triple "child’s play" must precede the "work of women." For children play with three things: First, frequently with very old gifts <note>original: "muneris... vetustissimis"; likely a coded reference to base matter or "primordial" substances</note>. Second, with urine. Third, with coals. The first play provides the material of the Stone. The second play increases the soul.

<margin>
blood salt
peter.
</margin>
The third play prepares the body for life: for from the flower of blood is made saltpeter <term>saltpeter: potassium nitrate, used here as a metaphor for a volatile mineral agent</term>, along with the first play of children. Once this is done, it remains to animate it, and frequently to dissolve it into water with its partner, using the two other plays of children, which are necessary up to the third heat of our elixir <term>elixir: the refined medicinal or transformative substance</term> in the work.

Albertus Magnus <note>a 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath</note> speaks thus concerning the generation of our stone: The place is the beginning of generation, and the place generates that which is placed within it through the properties of heaven, which properties flow into it through the roots of the stars. ### *To understand those things which enter into our work and mastery.*

Morienes <note>A 7th-century legendary alchemist known for his dialogues</note> says: Know that by "martyring" <note>original: "martirifando" – a term for intense heating or chemical distress</note> the bodies of minerals and spirits in the work—namely sulfur, arsenic, orpiment <note>original: "Auri pigmentum" – a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, etc.—which are known to the common people, they find absolutely nothing in them. I consider quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, sulfur, arsenic, or sal ammoniac <note>original: "sale armoniaco" – ammonium chloride</note> to be vain and useless; properly speaking, they are not spirits except in name, but are rather bodies, even though they are converted into smoke. In themselves, they have no constancy. Therefore, they cannot be the root in our blessed work; neither by themselves nor joined with anything else do they succeed or profit.

Johannes of Austria, the philosopher, says: Every body is either an element or composed of elements. But every composition and generation consists of four simple elements. Likewise, there are two active and two passive qualities. Two ascend, and the other two descend; one is in the middle, and another is beneath it. The reasoning for this is that a contrary is never joined with its opposite except through a medium <note>a middle or balancing element</note>. Therefore, that which is not contrary by its own nature is joined together. Just as the hot and the dry are joined by their own nature, since they are in no way opposed to each other—for those two elements, fire and air, are easily united together by their own nature—but the hot and the cold are not joined except through a medium, namely through the moist and the cold. This is because they cannot stand together by themselves, as one is always opposed to the other. For the moist and the cold consist well together, but the hot and the cold gather and scatter <term>homogeneous</term> <note>things of the same kind</note> substances, and not <term>heterogeneous</term> <note>things of different kinds</note> ones, by dissolving and congealing. However, the moist and the dry are gathered and scattered by constricting and moistening. Therefore, the operation of the elements is simple generation and natural transformation. It is thus manifest that all universal things are varied through heat and cold, and are simply generated and naturally transformed. For heat and cold give life to matter; but when the active forces are overcome, it is clear how they are variable according to their parts. Because anything does not just come from anything, but a specific thing comes from its own specific source, since no generation occurs except from things that are compatible in nature.

<margin>The proximity of metals</margin>
From this it follows that one element communicates its quality to another, so that by circulating its quality in this way, it can convert and transmute that quality into itself. It is also important to know that it is common to all metals that their matter is very close to one another in nature, in virtue, and in potential.

## Recapitulation of the entire work of *Alchemy*, 
### and of our stone according to the intention of all the philosophers.

**Plato** <note>The author likely refers to the 'Pseudo-Plato' of alchemical tradition rather than the classical Greek philosopher.</note> says, the Practitioner of our work must first dissolve the stone. Then, he must coagulate it, since our work is nothing other than making a perfect solution and coagulation. Whence the **Rosary** <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> says: Unless everything is turned into water, it can in no way reach perfection. Therefore, one must never use any mixing or grinding in the entire governance of our work, but only be occupied with the permanent water, the power of which is the spiritual blood—that is, the tincture <term>tincture: a potent liquid extract believed to transform base metals into gold</term> without which nothing happens. For in our operation, the body is converted into spirit, and the spirit into body. For in this way, the mixed things are reduced into one and unite with each other. For the body incorporates the spirit through the tincture of the blood, because everything that has spirit also has blood.

For every thing whose root is earth and water becomes dying. This is to say, the earth becomes water, and the qualities of the water overcome it; such is the dissolution of the body and the coagulation of the spirit, and vice versa. For they have one operation, because one is not dissolved unless the other is coagulated. Therefore, in the beginning of the work, you unite the sun <note>original: "so"; likely the start of "solem" (sun/gold), cut off by the page break.</note>

Therefore, Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says: The work of our stone is its own dissolution, knowing that in no way can the matter of the stone be destroyed without it remaining under some form.

### *The method of projection follows.*

How our stone <note>original: "lapis noster," the Philosopher's Stone or the completed alchemical elixir</note> ought to be projected onto metals. # RAYMOND

In terms of signifying the mind <note>original: "menti significãdo"</note>, a whole substance that is entirely compact and dry in its matter can never, according to the course of nature, be multiplied except through the resolution and thinning of its hard substance into simplicity. In such a hard and coagulated substance, the heat—being shut in and retained within—remains mortified <note>In alchemy, "mortified" refers to a state of inactivity or "death" where the active properties are bound and cannot act.</note> by reason of the dryness and hardness in which the matter is fixed. In this matter, the heat is held back because a mortifying quality is caused by the nature of extreme coldness and dryness. 
<margin>Mortified heat.</margin>
And therefore, such dryness requires an airy moistening to the end that the natural heat may be awakened and extended through the simple matter of the air, which is its natural food. 
<margin>Moisture brings forth heat; what kind of feeding.</margin>
But the reduction of these coarse parts into simple ones is not something nature can do through the thinning of its dry parts with resolution—which occurs through the "un-ripening" <note>original: "incrudationem," referring to returning a substance to a raw or "crude" state to restart its growth.</note> of the natural moisture of the grain, which had been finished and cooked with perfect digestion, in the manner of the subtle white substance from which the bread you eat is made. By this it is clear that nature does not pass from one contrary to another except through its middle point; through which middle point is caused the difference of harmony, by which nature converts from one nature into another. And this is the special difference that you must observe: that water is a friend to air through its moisture, and is a neighbor to earth through its coldness. 
<margin>The symbol of the elements.</margin>
Son, condensation and rarefaction <note>The process of making a substance more dense or more thin/porous.</note> are the original way in the transmutation of the elements through certain degrees; and it is the common difference by which wise nature converts the elements.

# TREATISE
## OF ARISTOTLE ON THE
### PRACTICE OF THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE

->It begins.<-

<margin>*The four natures.*</margin>
Since every body, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was frequently referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note>, is either an element or generated from the elements, generation is supremely necessary to our mastery. Furthermore, this generation cannot consist of anything except the four natures, which are the four elements. Indeed, the elements are four: air, water, fire, and earth, without which all generation is deprived of its effect. For of the elements, two are of a stony nature and two are of a watery nature; the stony ones are fire and earth, while the watery ones are air and water. Likewise, two of them are friends, and two are enemies. Earth and water are friends, while fire and water are enemies.

Therefore, make peace between the enemies, and you shall possess the whole mastery. But you cannot make peace between the elements except through their conversion into one another. Moreover, to convert them well into one another is entirely possible. Because, as the Philosopher says: It is within the aptitude of all elements that they be changed into one another. For fire is changed into air, and air into water. Thus fire is changed into water, and water into earth, and vice versa.

<summary>This introductory page establishes the elemental foundation of alchemy, arguing that the "mastery" of the Philosopher's Stone requires balancing and converting the four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—into one another.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Four Elements, Elemental Conversion, Natural Philosophy, Generation</keywords>

# ARISTOTLE

->Therefore, convert the elements, and you shall find what you seek.<- For our composition, as Morienus <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit, said to be the teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says, is a change of natures and a mixable connection of them: of the hot with the cold, and the moist with the dry. For the coldness of water, the heat of fire, the moisture of air, and the dryness of earth, being bound together in harmony, constitute the first complete generated thing. For the elements, as the Philosopher <note>In medieval texts, "The Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle.</note> says, are convertible in a circle. And for that reason, they are generated and corrupted by one another, but this is not accomplished except by operation and governance.

The modes of operations are four: namely, the <gloss>1</gloss>dissolution of the stone into spiritual water, the <gloss>2</gloss>separation of the stone into a spiritual state, the <gloss>3</gloss>reduction of the stone into natural earth, and the <gloss>4</gloss>betrothal of the stone into a spiritual lime <note>The term "lime" or "calx" refers to a powder produced by heating a substance until it loses its moisture and becomes friable.</note>.

<margin>solution <unclear>reasoning</unclear></margin>

The dissolution of the stone is done by grinding; the separation of the stone by distillation; the reduction of the stone by waxing <note>original: "incerationem" — a process of adding liquid to a dry substance to give it a soft, wax-like consistency.</note>; and the betrothal by fixation.

The first step of our governance or work is therefore the dissolution of the stone into spiritual water, as the philosopher says. Since the first mode of preparation is that the stone becomes Mercury. For Mercury itself is the first body operating on coarse things, so that it may return them to its own likeness. For if one were to leave coarse things in their coarseness, and did not refine the being, the stone would neither be dissolved nor would it rot. And therefore if another...

# A LITTLE TREATISE

Even if we received no other benefit from Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; in alchemy, Mercury represents the fluid, transformative principle of matter</note> except that it renders bodies subtle according to its own nature, that should be sufficient for us. Therefore, take your most beloved son and join him equally to his white sister; offer them the cup of love, because the consensus of goodwill joins things to things. <margin>A loving conjunction.</margin> Pour honeyed wine over them until they are intoxicated and divided into the smallest parts. Nevertheless, keep in mind that all clean things suit clean things; otherwise, they generate sons unlike themselves.

And for that reason, as Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher whose writings were foundational to medieval alchemy</note> says: The first thing you must do in the work is to sublime the Mercury. Then, place clean bodies into the clean Mercury; thereafter, grind, cook, and repeat, and do not let this task weary you. When you truly see blackness appearing on the surface of the water, collect it carefully and set it aside, knowing for certain that your stone is now partially dissolved. Distill all the water through a cloth; that which you find dissolved in it, set aside, and put the remainder back to be cooked again until the whole thing turns black in the manner of soot. Let all these things be done with a temperate fire of the first degree, warm and moist. For if excessive heat is present, it will turn the blackness into redness <margin>The Raven's Head.</margin> <note>original: "Caput corui"; a traditional alchemical term for the black stage of decomposition</note>, and the heat of hasty redness is a sign of combustion. And therefore, if you have governed the origin of the art well, it will be the "Raven's Head," for in that state the body is dissolved and reduced into its primary matter. And for that reason...

Because, as Aristotle says, bodies are not altered unless they are first reduced into <term>prime matter</term> <note>The fundamental, formless substance from which all things are made</note>. And therefore, as Plato says, you have need to labor in their solution, so that once the heavier parts are cast away, the work may be completed with the lighter ones. This is indeed accomplished through <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</note>. And this is because the blood is the soul; and the soul is life, and life is our <term>stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the alchemical Great Work</note>. For nothing is suitable for our stone which has not been alive and has not sought the heaven of the air. Therefore, convert your stone into blood, and blood into air, and air into earth, and you shall have the whole <term>mastery</term> <note>The completed alchemical process or secret knowledge</note>.

The second step of our governance is the separation of the stone into a spiritual state. This separation is achieved through the division of the elements and their full purification.

Regarding the purification of the separation, as Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis," a famous Persian alchemist and physician</note> says: It is necessary to divide the natures of the stone into the four elements and to cleanse them individually through distillation. For fire extracts that which dwells in the inner parts. It consumes the filth of the stone through distillation and refines it through the lightening of the air; and therefore our stone is divided into four elements so that it may be more refined, better purified from filth, and more firmly joined together afterward. Putrefaction must necessarily precede division, <margin>putrefaction before division</margin> so that the elemental parts within it may be dissolved, and thus it is rendered more fit afterwards for extraction through the four elements. <margin><unclear>blackness</unclear></margin>
For as the philosopher says: Corruption is the putrefaction of the substance of a thing, resulting from the retention of vapor and the action of fire. For the first thing that distills, as Avicenna <note>original: "Auicēna"; a highly influential Persian polymath and philosopher</note> says, is water, but it is not yet pure. Afterwards, fire mixed with air drips out. Keep those together until you divide them. That which remains burned at the bottom is the black and dry earth.

Therefore, join part with part at all times, and preserve each of them individually; this is the correct separation of the elements and a complete purification. For in our work, no water is necessary unless it is white, nor air unless it is saffron-yellow, nor earth unless it is pale and whitish. For then the water is fit for dissolving and effective for entering, and the air is overflowing for staining the oil. Divide your stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone" or the primary material of the work</note> therefore into four elements, rectify them, and join them into one, and you will possess the entire mastery <term>Magisterium: the complete process or "Great Work" of alchemy</term>.

<margin>How inceration is performed.</margin> The third step of our work, therefore, is the reduction of the stone into natural earth. This reduction is achieved through the grinding of the earth and the "inceration" <term>Inceration: a process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it reaches a wax-like consistency</term> of water upon it. The inceration of water is to restore moisture to the parts of the earth that were deprived of it through calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</note>, and to make it like soil. For a dry and clean body is suitable for drinking, since every dry thing hungers for its own moisture. Therefore, tie the hands of the nursing woman behind her back so that she cannot strike the son; place a toad <note>The "toad" is a common alchemical symbol for the heavy, poisonous, or earthy matter at the bottom of a vessel</note> upon her hands so that it may nurse from her until it dies, and the woman...

<margin>Light calcination.</margin>
over it more water, as before; cook it gently for a week, calcine it gently, and again put it back with new water for cooking. Do this continually until the earth has consumed ten times its own weight of water.

For all things crave water, since water itself provides nourishment to fire as well as to other things, and it embraces a secret worthy of admiration. For it is the wine in the vine, the oil in the olive tree, and through water, fruits of various kinds are transformed upon the tree. So also in our earth, [the stone] is generated from water; for water itself is cold and is called quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; here referring to the philosophical Mercury or the transformative liquid principle</note>, which is hidden in the body of magnesia <note>term: magnesia (a common alchemical term for the crude mineral or "mother" of the stone, not necessarily modern magnesium)</note> and is to be congealed within it. Therefore, when it is congealed, it is made like unto ashes, because the earth dries and the water moistens. And for that reason, the weight must be noted everywhere, lest administering too much dryness or superfluous moisture should corrupt the work; namely, that you should cook away by roasting as much as the dissolution added, and dissolve by moistening as much as was lost by roasting. And therefore, every time after the calcination of the earth, pour the water over it temperately—neither too much nor too little—because if there is too much, it will become a sea of perturbation <note>original: "pelagus conturbationis"; a state of chaotic imbalance where the solid matter is drowned and cannot be fixed</note>; but if indeed...

The double way:
Universal
Particular

According to the Philosophers, there is a double way in this art: namely, the universal and the particular.

<margin>
Sudden coagulation of Mercury.
</margin>
The universal way is easy and rare; it is that which is drawn forth from true and natural principles. By these, a seminative and reformative virtue immediately, and in a moment, hardens Mercury <note>The metal Quicksilver, considered the "mother" of all metals in alchemy.</note> and tints any properly prepared metal into true gold or silver, according to how that primordial virtue was directed toward its end by the joining of active things to passive things.

<margin>
The natural way.
</margin>
The second way, however, is called particular, and it is difficult and laborious. Note that although Alchemy in the universal way is partly natural and partly artificial, it is nevertheless more natural. This is because in the way of true Alchemy, nature introduces nothing foreign or strange; nature possesses that upon which it works, because actives are joined to passives through a competent union or application, and nature performs the rest by itself. Plato says: our stone is a thing which fire has not touched, from which our Mercury rises.

# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
## The properties of their qualities.

<margin>The quality of the stone.</margin>
First, that it must possess within itself a most subtle and incombustible earth, which is fit for fixing <note>In alchemy, "fixing" refers to making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat.</note> and is entirely fixed with its own proper radical moisture <note>The "radical moisture" was believed to be the fundamental life-fluid or essential sap of a substance.</note>.

Second: it must have an airy and fiery humidity, uniformly joined together, so that if one part were volatile, the other would be as well. And this humidity is superior to all other humidities, enduring the heat of the fire until the completion of its sufficient thickening into ash, according to its need, remaining inseparably joined to the attached earth without evaporating.

Third, that the natural disposition of the humidity be such that, by the benefit of its homogeneity <note>term: homogeneity (the state of being all of the same kind; here, the perfect blending of elements)</note> across all its different properties, it holds the earth annexed by the conversion of both. Because they are virtuously tempered in each other's homogeneity and total union, and by a bond of inseparable connection, they should equally provide a good fusion <note>original: "fusionem," referring to the ability to melt or flow like wax</note> after the final stage of preparation.

Fourth, that this homogeneity be of such purity of essence, and artificially cleansed of every combustible or burning thing, that it does not burn the things with which it is joined down to their smallest parts, but rather preserves them from combustion.

Fifth, that it should have within itself a clear and splendid tincture <note>term: tincture (a potent medicinal or alchemical essence capable of changing the color and nature of a substance)</note>, either white or red, clean and incombustible, stable and fixed, such that fire is in no way able to change it.

<margin>The First Matter</margin>
The first matter <note>Latin: *prima materia*; the fundamental substance from which all things are made</note> of bodies is not the common Mercury <note>The liquid metal quicksilver found in shops</note>, but is an unctuous and moist vapor. For from the moist part the mineral stone is made, and from the unctuous part the metallic body is formed. Indeed, it is necessary that bodies be converted into such an unctuous vapor; and in this conversion, the bodies are destroyed, and the grain of the body is cast down into death and totally mortified. And this is accomplished by means of our white and red water. And understand it thus: unless a grain of wheat <note>A biblical metaphor from John 12:24 used here to describe the "death" of the metal before its rebirth</note>—that is, the grain of the body—is cast into the earth—that is, into its first matter, which is the unctuous vapor or the Mercury of the Philosophers <margin>the vapor is our stone</margin> and of the wise, etc. And such a vapor is called "the stone" in the well-known chapters of books, and the beginning of the matter of our operation, and the unctuous sulfur, from which, at the completion, the quintessence <note>The "fifth essence" or purest state of matter</note> is extracted: the Mercury, tinting every body into Sun <note>Gold</note> or Moon <note>Silver</note>, according to how the stone was finally prepared.

<margin>Ferment</margin>
pure gold has been led through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body, and to ferment further with it is entirely impossible according to the Philosophers, unless one possesses the **First Matter** <note>original: "materia prima"; the primordial, formless substance from which all elements were thought to originate</note> of metals, in which the gold may be resolved back into its first matter and into its miscible elements. Let us therefore take that matter from which gold is made, and by means of artifice, it is led into the true **ferment of the philosophers**. And let us change this with ingenuity into a perfected matter, or into the spirit of perfected bodies. For this reason, many among the moderns—even those laboring as Philosophers—are deceived, because they abandon the work at the very point where it should be beginning. Alas for you, sons of

doctrine, who hope to gather fruit before it is ripe, and hope to reap before the harvest! Another Philosopher says: From the perfect, nothing can be made, since a species of thing that is perfect in its nature does not change, but rather [remains].

## THE ARRANGEMENT OF THE VESSEL
### *suitable for our work according to the tradition*
### *stated by a certain blacksmith by name.*

<margin>The vessel of the work</margin>
Let a round glass shell <note>original: "concha vitrea"</note> be made, the bottom of which should be of small size in the manner of a side-dish or platter. And in the middle of it, let a glass belt <note>original: "zona vitrea"</note> be formed as a spindle-ring surrounding it. And upon that belt, let a round wall be cast, equally distant from the wall of the shell to the thickness of the cover of the shell itself, so that the wall of the cover may fall into this distance loosely without pressure. Let the height of this wall be according to the measure of the height of the shell's wall, either a little more or a little less. Let two covers be formed equal to the measure of this cavity of the two walls, the length of which should be equal, and let each be the size of two large palms <note>a "palm" was a traditional unit of measurement based on the width of the hand</note>. Their shape should be the same, namely pyramidal. In their heads let there be two equal holes, one in one and the other in the other, into both of which a single hen's feather <note>The catchword "penna" (feather) at the bottom of the original page indicates the next word in the sequence.</note>

# THE ROSARY

...convert the living silver <note>original: "argentum vivum," commonly known as quicksilver or mercury</note> into the nature of the sun, just as leaven converts the whole dough into the nature of the leaven; however, it does not happen the other way around, because the dominated is always transferred to the dominant. The Stone of the Philosophers is made from three things: namely, the sun, the moon, and Mercury. That is to say, make Mercury from the sun and the moon in its own being without the common mercury of the masses, but through the philosophical way. Note: This stone is one in the whole world, and whoever errs from this one thing at the beginning of the work labors in vain. In the whole world there <margin>The unique stone.</margin> is no other thing necessary in our work except this stone given to us alone, the sons of art. Arnold <note>referring to Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century alchemist and physician</note> says: In our stone, the sun and moon are present in virtue and power, and also in nature. If this were not so, neither the sun nor the moon would be produced from it, because the sun and moon in our stone are better than the common versions in their own nature; this is because the sun and moon in our stone are living, while the common ones are dead in comparison to the sun and moon in our stone. Therefore, the philosophers named the stone itself "sun and moon" interchangeably, because they are in it potentially and not visibly, but in virtue and in essence. Wherefore Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many alchemical works are attributed</note> says: Because our stone cries out, saying, "Son, help me, and I will help you."

It emphasizes the internal power of the Stone to transform matter, likened to the action of leaven in bread.</summary>

# THE ROSARY II

In the same way, water is thickened with earth, and it becomes just like dense earth because earth is thicker than water. Therefore, there is no difference between the <term>dissolution of the body</term><note>The process of turning a solid metal into a liquid state</note> and the <term>coagulation of the spirit</term><note>The process of fixing a volatile substance into a solid state</note>, nor is there any diverse work in either, so that one might happen without the other. Just as there is no separate span of time between water and earth in their joining—where one might be recognized or separated from the other in their operations—so too the seed of the man is not separated from the seed of the woman at the hour of their coitus. Thus, they share one limit, one deed, and one and the same operation perceived simultaneously upon them both.

For when males lead the females, nature rejoices and a true generation occurs; however, when a nature is joined to an unsuitable foreign nature, it begets no true seed.
This is what Merculinus says.

Philosophical Putrefaction is nothing other than the corruption or destruction of bodies. For when one form is destroyed, nature immediately introduces another form into itself, one that is better and more subtle. Putrefaction is the same as the breaking of the putrid. For a pure, putrefied body immediately grows and multiplies into its own likeness, as is evident in a grain of seed; after it has remained for many days under the heat of the earth, it swells so that what is pure may grow and multiply from it, while the foulness vanishes. Therefore, putrefaction is also necessary in our work for the aforementioned reasons.

### The Time for the Perfection of the Stone

I ask in how much time this blessed stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary goal of alchemy</note> can be made, to which it is answered that a certain author, the Philosopher Lilius, testifies that he completed his mastery in eight days; some say in seven, some in three months, others in four, others in half a year, and others in one year. And Maria <note>Maria the Jewess, an early alchemical authority</note> says she did it in three days. To this I say that the cause of this diversity—namely the brevity or prolongation—could be a defect in the power of the Mercury-water. Or perhaps because they were working with the Sun and the Moon. <note>In alchemy, "Sun" refers to Gold and "Moon" to Silver.</note>

<margin>The diversity of the laborers</margin>

The spirit was fixed from the body. And then the spirit was fixed in the body, and the Moon <note>original: "luna"; refers to Silver or the feminine principle</note> was incorporated into the Sun <note>original: "soli"; refers to Gold or the masculine principle</note>, and they were mixed together through the smallest parts, and thus the work was completed. From this arose a diversity in the method of acting; the work could be done by adding more of the fixed body than the non-fixed, or vice versa, because <gloss>since</gloss> when there was more of the non-fixed it ascended more quickly, and when there was more of the fixed it ascended more slowly.

But what do you say concerning that which the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemists</note> say, namely: "Our Gold is not common gold, and our Silver is not common silver"? I say that they call the "water" Gold, because by the power of fire it ascends to the higher parts. And truly that Gold is not the gold of the common people, for the common people would not believe it could ascend to the higher parts on account of its fixedness. Know furthermore that, by God, such has always been the custom of the Philosophers: namely, to limp at the most certain passage, and to hide a thing that has been stated—sometimes through symbols and figures, sometimes through metaphorical words, and sometimes through a false and foreign practice. And where they felt they had spoken the truth, they would then say they had spoken figuratively. Hence Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a famous 8th-century alchemist</note> says: "Wherever we have spoken openly, there we have said nothing. But where we have placed something under a riddle..."

# THE ROSARY

->Solomon, in the Seventh Chapter of Wisdom.<-

He proposed to hold this science <note>original: "scientiam"; here referring to the Alchemical Art or Wisdom</note> in place of light, and above all beauty and health. In comparison to that precious stone, he did not compare it <note>the stone</note> to anything else, because all gold is like a small grain of sand, and silver shall be esteemed as clay in its sight. For its acquisition is better than the trading of silver and of gold, even the pure and the most refined. Its fruit is more precious than all the riches of this world, and all things that are desired in the world cannot be compared to it. Length of days and health are in its right hand, and in its left hand are glory and infinite riches. Its ways are beautiful and praiseworthy operations, not to be despised, and its paths are measured and not hasty, but achieved with the persistence of long-lasting labor; it is a tree of life to those who grasp it, and an unfailing light; blessed are those who shall hold it, because the science of God shall never perish, as Alphidius <note>An Arab alchemist often cited in medieval texts</note> testifies, saying: He who finds this science, his food shall be lawful and everlasting.

Aristotle: Oh, how wonderful is that thing which has in itself all that we seek, to which we add nothing and from which we diminish nothing, but in the preparation alone we remove the superfluities.

<margin>Mortification <note>The alchemical process of "killing" or breaking down a substance to its base components.</note></margin>
Mortification is the separation of hardness from the body, because the soul is then dead, yet the body is alive by reason of heat and dryness. For everything possessing heat possesses life. And for this reason, alchemical lime <note>original: "calx alchimica"; refers to the powdery residue left after heating a metal or mineral.</note> is said to possess life, because the philosophers have striven to kill that imperfect life of theirs, and to restore a perpetual life.

<margin>Revivification <note>The "bringing back to life" or restoration of the substance in a perfected state.</note></margin>
Revivification is by reason of nourishment—namely, of its own perfected moisture—and the restoration of the rectifying humidity by the removal of that same imperfect moisture.

<margin>Sublimation is twofold.</margin>

# THE ROSARY

<margin>What the Elixir is</margin>
It is the elixir, and it is called the stone that is not a stone <note>Latin: *lapis non lapis*; a common alchemical paradox describing a substance that is physically solid like a stone but possesses the transformative properties of a liquid or spirit</note>; a stone because it can be ground, but not a stone because it melts. And it flows without evaporating, just like gold, nor is there any other thing to which that property belongs. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy</note> says: The elixir is therefore a thing which is projected upon a greater body, and it changes that thing from its own nature into another. Moreover, it is made when a lesser body and spirit and elements and ferment are mixed together, and one preparation is made from them all. And "Elixir" is a Greek word <note>The author incorrectly attributes the origin to Greek; it actually derives from the Arabic *al-iksīr*</note> which signifies a "great treasure," or the "best of treasures." And indeed, the Elixir which mixes itself with a body is like Tutia <term>Tutia: an impure form of zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term> with Copper. But the Copper is augmented or grows from that Tutia; the reason for this is because Tutia is an earthy thing, while the Elixir is a spiritual thing, and the nature of its kind is turned back toward another kind.

The Alchemist: Moreover, the Elixir is made in two ways. In one way, from mineral spirits and prepared clean bodies. In the other way, from certain things originating from living beings, namely from hair, or an egg, or blood, etc.

In the first way, it is done thus: certain spirits are "killed" <note>original: *mortificantur*; refers to the process of changing a substance's chemical state so it loses its original outward characteristics</note> and sublimated <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</term> until they become clean. After this, one of the bodies generated by nature is burned until it can be ground; then it is calcined <term>calcination: reducing a metal or mineral to a fine powder or ash through high heat</term> until it is made clean in the manner of lime.

Finally, the spirits and bodies prepared in this way are ground and soaked with distilled sharp waters <note>original: *aquis acutis*; likely referring to acids or caustic solutions used as solvents</note>...

## ON THE COMPLETION OF THE ELIXIR.

<margin>
The Elixir for the Red is desired, but it is finished by three parts.
</margin>

Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical works were foundational in Europe</note> in his letter to Hasen: The Elixir, therefore, tints with its tincture, is submerged by its oil, and is fixed by its lime <note>original: "calce"; the powdered residue left after heating a substance</note>. The Gloss: It is true that the White Elixir requires nothing but three things, namely oil, tincture, and lime. But the Red requires four: oil, lime, tincture, and again a tincture which is called "fire." And for this reason, Avicenna adds, "in which there is no fire" <note>referring to the specific composition of the White stage versus the Red</note>.

## ON THE MULTIPLE FIRE.

There is, however, a multiple Fire, and its quality is diverse, distinguished by certain degrees. For one fire is hot in the first degree and moist in the second, namely the "horse’s belly" <note>original: "ventris equi"; a term for the gentle, moist heat produced by fermenting horse manure, used for slow digestion of materials</note>, the property of which is that it does not destroy the oil but increases it because of its moisture. For other fires destroy it because of their dryness.
<margin>The fire of a healthy person.</margin>
Therefore, no other fire in the world is likened to this except for the material fire of a healthy human body. Indeed, the fire of the Sun is hot in the same degree, but it is dry.
<margin>The taming fire.</margin>
This, however, is the fire that tames the matter; it is made from a living thing and is nourished by it.

just like a child who is given milk in the beginning. <margin>*The fifth.*</margin>

fire of the melting furnace in that same degree.
There is also the fire of the bellows, which dissipates, scatters, and melts bodies, and this is the seventh.

# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS

<margin>The Eighth.</margin>
The eighth type of fire is that which melts and calcines <note>calcinat: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances or reduce it to powder</note>, and it is a flaming fire, because in this type, the flame alone performs the work. The substance of fire consists of coals and flame, but in this specific type, it is only the flame of the wood. This fire is also at the same level of intensity as the preceding ones.

<margin>The Ninth.</margin>
At the same level is the ninth, which is the master of all: namely the fire of "officiation," which is to say, the fire of examination <note>original: "examinationis" – the process of testing the purity of metals</note>. This fire melts and burns; it dissipates and scatters the bad, while it saves and rectifies the good. It is like a judge discerning the just from the unjust.

## OF JUNIPERS

->Fire.<-

An artificial fire that is continuous and lasting, remaining at whatever degree of heat you wish for one, two, or three months, until you expose the coals; therefore, you must always keep them covered. You can increase or decrease the heat at your pleasure, according to the addition of more or fewer lit coals. First, you must have sufficient ashes, made solely from juniper wood. Then, take a large earthen pot, in the middle of which is another smaller pot or crucible <term>crucibulum: a vessel used for melting substances at very high temperatures</term>. In placing the ashes, let the large pot stand over the heat of a fire until the ash itself grows hot. Then, all around the smaller pot, place coals upon the ashes, which are also made only from the aforementioned juniper wood.

Finally, have even more heated ashes ready...

## GENERAL RULES.

Every thing is composed of that into which it is resolved; for as ice is converted into water by means of heat, it is therefore necessary that it was water before it was ice. Thus all metals were previously quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum" (living silver). Alchemists believed mercury was the "first matter" or mother of all metals.</note>, which is evident because when they melt in the fire, they are converted into it. Note here that the philosopher also calls a melted metal "mercury" or "quicksilver"; therefore, the reduction of metals into quicksilver in this manner is called "liquation" <note>The process of melting or becoming liquid.</note>. Although this happens through the violence of fire, nevertheless, because in that intense melting it maintains the appearance of quicksilver, he therefore names it quicksilver. But this is not the *philosophical* solution, but rather the *layman's* solution; therefore, it corresponds in some way to the sayings of philosophy regarding the particular things known to you.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and alchemical axioms from the previous section of the Rosarium, focusing on the fundamental laws of nature that govern the transformation of matter.</meta>

The Second Rule. Every nature naturally desires to be perfected and abhors and flees from being destroyed; therefore, it greedily embraces that which is corrective of itself, and rejects its contrary as much as it can. According to this principle, art <note>In this context, "art" refers to Alchemy, the practical application of human skill to natural processes.</note> must imitate nature, otherwise it always errs.

# THE THIRD RULE.

Everything of a worse quality working in any art strives by its own natural malice to destroy the better; and everything of a better quality working in any art endeavors to perfect the worse. Therefore, you must first know the natures of things, so that you may know how to discern what is better or worse for a nature, and from what it may be perfected and by what it may be hindered. You must also ensure that the quantity of the worse does not exceed the quantity of the better; otherwise, you will err greatly.

# THE FOURTH RULE.

Everything dry naturally desires to drink its own moisture so that it may be joined together in its parts. Note here what the radical moisture <note>original: "humidum radicale" — the fundamental, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist within all metals and living things.</note> of all liquefiable things <term>liquabilium</term> <note>Substances capable of being melted or dissolved.</note> is; feed the overly dry with such moisture, and it will become tempered, and so on.

->And thus you shall have what you desired.<-

## ON THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN
### *common sulfur and the simple, non-burning*
#### *sulfur of the Philosophers.*

---

<margin>Our sulfur.</margin>
<margin>Common sulfur.</margin>
<margin>The nature of the philosophers' fire.</margin>
<margin>Maturing and life-giving.</margin>
<margin>Supplying the defects of nature.</margin>

**W**hen the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, often cited simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> speaks generally, saying that sulfur coagulates, it must be said that this is not the case [with common sulfur], because all common sulfur, according to the philosopher, is foreign and contrary to metals. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and polymath whose alchemical writings were highly influential in Europe.</note> says: Nothing enters into the mastery <note>original: "magisterium" — the Great Work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> which did not originate from it, because it always infects, blackens, and corrupts in whatever way it may be prepared by art. For it is itself an infected fire, and therefore it hinders fusion. If, however, it is calcined <note>term: calcination — the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve decomposition or oxidation.</note>, it returns to an earthy substance like a dead powder. How, then, can it inspire life in others? For it possesses a double superfluity: namely, an inflammable substance and an earthy dross. Therefore, by these things consider that these are the sulfurs of the common people and not of the philosophers, since the sulfur of the philosophers is a simple living fire, giving life to other dead bodies and maturing them, so that it supplies the defect of nature; for it is of a redundant maturity, according to which it is perfect in its own nature, and by art it is made more and more...

# HOW RED SUL-
## phur is in the sun, and
### white in the moon.

Since it has been said that the sulfur of the philosophers exists as red in the sun <note>In alchemy, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold.</note> through greater digestion, and white sulfur exists in the moon <note>The Moon (Luna) represents Silver.</note> through lesser digestion, hence <margin>Yellowing</margin> the philosopher says: yellowing <note>original: "citrinatio"; the third stage of the alchemical process, following blackening and whitening.</note> is nothing other than complete digestion. For heat acting upon the moist first generates blackness, and acting upon the dry it causes whiteness; because if the fire surpasses this, acting upon it, it changes into the purest yellow. All these things can be observed in the calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to cause oxidation or change in texture.</note> of lead. And the philosopher says that each of the perfect bodies already contains its own good sulfur with mercury: namely, gold contains golden sulfur, and silver contains silvery sulfur. Therefore, white sulfur through the yellow is gold, wherefore the sulfur in it is red sulfur, the substance of fire, which has digested this white further. And thus, white and red sulfur exist on both sides within the sun; for which reason fire is its perfection, and it was generated in fire, and therefore it amicably endures the nature of its own fire.

# THE ROSARY

Therefore, certain external things cannot cause this in bodies, since art is nothing other than the mediation of nature <note>The author argues that alchemy does not "cheat" nature, but uses natural laws more efficiently.</note>, except for the cooking and digestion of that nature through simple labor. For example: in the morning when I rise and see my urine is white, I judge that I have slept too little. Then I lay myself down again to sleep, and having taken my sleep, the urine becomes lemon-colored <note>original: "citrinatur"; a key alchemical stage signifying maturation</note>. <margin>The cause of lemon-coloring</margin>

In this way, follow nature through art to similarly cook, digest, ripen, and sublime <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then cooling it back to a solid to purify it</term>, since nature already contains within itself the natural fire by which it is ripened. Those external things do not possess this fire, and therefore they cannot give it. 

<margin>Exhortation</margin>

In Silver <note>original: "luna" (the Moon), the alchemical symbol for silver</note>, however, there is nothing but white sulfur, which is simple; yet it is not digested like the red sulfur, nor is it so purged of blackness through the action of heat which it naturally contains within itself. Rather, the species of fire is covered and hidden, acting upon it in art as in nature and vice versa. 

<margin>Note the ripening fire</margin>

And therefore it is not impossible that art, through the mediation of nature—note here the "mediating nature" or "middle nature"—should further digest and perfect it, since it naturally intends to be perfected. However, it cannot do this by itself unless it is moved by art and manual operation. But these labors, as I believe, will not reach a stiff-necked man <note>A biblical idiom for someone stubborn or spiritually blind</note>. Therefore, true Gold is not made unless it is so digested and cooked that the better part improves the worse. 

<margin>The better perfects the worse</margin>

For the intention of all the philosophers is to perfect the worse with the better.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the fundamental composition of metals and why lesser minerals cannot be transformed into true metals.</meta>

->OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.<-

The matter of these things, which is mercury <note>original: "mercurius"; here referring to the alchemical principle of Quicksilver</note>, is not generated from them, because their generation differs from the generation of mercury primarily in form, in nature, and in composition. Therefore, metals cannot be made from them because for things of one species, there is one primary matter and seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> from which they are generated. The first part of the preceding argument is clear: that the lesser minerals are not generative from mercury. The reason is because mercury always remains in the primary matter of metals and does not contain foreign sulfurs.

Hence Aristotle and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose works on medicine and alchemy were foundational in the West</note> state: Therefore, if metals were to be made, it would be necessary that they first pass into the primary matter of metals. But because this cannot be done artificially, metals can by no means be made from them. Thus the first part of the preceding argument is sufficiently declared.

Secondly, regarding the same point: because the lesser minerals—the principle of metals—cannot be made artificially (which is mercury), they therefore do not reach the middle and the end, which are the metal and the tincture <note>term: tincture (a potent alchemical substance capable of transmuting or coloring metals)</note>. This holds true because nourishment in a human cannot become a human through generation unless it is first converted into seed; and thus, added to its like, a new human is generated. But because the lesser minerals are of a foreign nature to metals—even though they participate well enough in some mineral force—they are of a weaker virtue and are combustible. Therefore, the metallic nature does not delight in them,
<margin>Nature does not delight in the mineral spirit.</margin>
but rejects them and preserves those things which are of its own nature. For example: if water were mixed with earth, they are separated from one another, because the earth seeks the bottom since it is heavy and dry, while the water seeks the surface.

# WHAT ARE THE
## particulars which are perfected
### in this art.

To all observers into whose hands these present discourses may come, I declare universally that in the entire sequence of this art there are only two particulars which are perfected in a specific way according to the philosophers and nature. The first particular, existing in both the white <note>The 'albedo' or silver-making stage.</note> and the red <note>The 'rubedo' or gold-making stage.</note>, exists in mercury <term>mercury: the fluid principle of matter</term> without the administration of the "perfect medicine," although the body with which it is perfected contains within itself the hidden tincture of that very thing, just as nature requires. The first reason that it exists particularly in him <insert>mercury</insert> from both species of things is this: since mercury is composed of the first matter of all metals—from a very sulfurous white earth and clear water—therefore the whiteness of the earth shines through the clarity of the water, and the color in it is the brightest white.

Proceed to universal matters. For the putrefaction of all natures bound together is their dissolution and separation; thus, the bound parts are separated from one another, and each part from the next. This occurs through the separation and dissolution of the **elements** <term>elements: the four building blocks of matter—earth, water, air, and fire</term> which are connected in the generation of mercury—namely, water and earth. This separation cannot occur in bodies except through the **spirit**. Thus, art transcends nature in one way: namely, that artificial things may be well and suddenly accomplished, which previously were naturally prolonged.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion of the relationship between Art (human skill/alchemy) and Nature, specifically focusing on the limits of elemental transmutation and the role of Mercury as the foundational "root" of metals.</meta>

# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS

When the elements that existed are transmuted, since the primary nature has changed one quality into another, Art is well able to separate them—such as the moist from the dry, or the cold from the hot. However, one quality still possesses the nature of another in some part due to their natural mixture. Through this, they can be joined back together by Art just as they were divided. If it were not the case that one quality participated in the nature of another—namely, water sharing the nature <margin>On the first matter.</margin> of earth in its coldness, and air sharing the nature of water in its moisture, and so forth—then it would follow that the work of nature would be totally destroyed. Since the elements would then be in their simplest state, just as they were before the generation of Mercury <note>original: "mercurij"; here referring to "Quicksilver" or the philosophical principle of liquidity and transformation</note>, Art would have destroyed nature by beginning from the head—namely, from gold and silver—down to the beginning, that is, to quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>. To go beyond these principles of the simple elements, back to how they were before the generation of Mercury, is impossible in Art because it is so remote. <margin>The possibility of Art.</margin> If it were possible, it would then follow that Art could compose elements anew out of the "first matter" <term>First Matter: the formless primordial substance from which all things are created</term> of metals; and conversely, Art would generate Mercury just as it destroyed it, which is impossible to be done artificially. Indeed, Art destroys from the head down to the feet—that is, from the finished metal down to Mercury—building from the foot up to the head in a more subtle form, granted that the substance of nature existed before the Art. Thus are the species of things divided, when they are transmuted into another form than they were before.

# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
## SECOND PART

<gloss>The matter is found in the sun, in mercury, and in the sulfur of the philosophers.</gloss> <note>original: "re est in sole, mercurio, & sulphure philosophorum." The 'sun' refers to gold, and 'mercury' and 'sulfur' are the two primary principles of alchemy.</note>
Since it was stated above that the moon <note>Silver</note> contains within itself white sulfur just as gold contains red sulfur, yet the appearance of fire is hidden within it beneath that whiteness; therefore, it is possible for all silver to become gold. Whence the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: "there is no gold unless it was first silver." Thus, silver contains within itself certain undigested qualities which can be purged from it by the Art, so that it passes specifically into fixed mercury and into the closest nature of gold. This is because it then contains within itself everything that gold does, through the application of the red sulfur of the philosophers, by which it is further digested. A yellowing <note>original: "citrinatio," the process of turning silver-colored matter into gold-colored matter</note> is caused within it by the addition of the perfect body <note>Gold</note>, since they are simply of one and the same nature. However, it is impossible for this to happen in other bodies <note>Base metals like lead or iron</note>, as they do not possess such a close proximity to the perfect nature as silver does. Their development is hindered during their generation by combustible and foul-smelling sulfur. Nor are they made of the mercury of which the philosopher speaks: "there is no passage from one extreme to the other except through the middle." That is to say, gold is not generated from mercury unless it was first silver. Nor do those other bodies contain the sulfur of simple, non-burning fire, but rather a scorching sulfur; therefore, they cannot be transformed specifically into fixed mercury, as was said above by Aristotle: "Let the craftsmen know <note>original: "Sciant artifices," a famous opening to a medieval alchemical text attributed to Aristotle</note> that they can only make things similar to them, and tint them..."

Therefore, it fails more slowly in the fire than lead or tin, because the mercury resists, except for the violence it suffers from the sulfur mixed with it. But as for the fact that lead is burned more quickly, this is by reason of the infected mercury, because infected mercury with infected sulfur is exactly what lead is.

<margin>The nature of Salt.</margin>

# HOW METALS ARE GENERATED
## from Mercury
### *specifically.*

<margin>The coagulation of mercury.</margin>
The nature of all liquefiable things is from quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note> and its own substance. This is because it is the property of quicksilver to be coagulated by the vapor or heat of white or red sulfur that does not burn. Whence Aristotle says in the fourth book of *Meteorology* <note>original: "metheororū"; a reference to the Aristotelian work on natural phenomena</note>: if the sulfur is white and non-burning, it congeals mercury into good silver. If, however, the sulfur is pure, with a clear redness, and contains the power of a simple non-burning fire, it congeals it into the purest gold—better than that which the mine produces. This is because every dry thing naturally drinks up its own moisture so that it may be joined in its parts. Therefore, the vapor of the sulfur of quicksilver is to be coagulated from a subtle, airy, earthy substance, boiled and undigested from the first mixture, united to itself by the action of heat; afterwards it is elevated, boiled, and digested until it possesses the sulfurous power of coagulating quicksilver into metallic bodies. Gold possesses much of the virtue of sulfur and
