For this reason, on account of the mercury, it is extremely heavy; and on account of the sulfurous power, it is very red. Silver <note>original: "argentum"</note>, however, behaves in a contrary manner in all respects, because it has much of the substance of sulfur and little of its power, and little of the substance of mercury and much of its power. Therefore it is white, because color follows the abundance of the power, and the power is located in the vapor. Its matter is closer to the matter of gold than any other metal; therefore, it is easily turned into gold, requiring no other labor except for transforming the color and adding weight.

## THE DIFFERENCE OF OIL
### and water in the method of
### dyeing.
### Arnold <note>Likely referring to Arnold of Villanova, a famous 13th-century alchemist and physician.</note>.

<margin>Difference between the Dye of Water and Oil</margin>
There is a difference between the dyeing <term>tincture</term> <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is a substance capable of infusing its properties or colors into another body.</note> of water and of oil, because water only washes and cleanses, while oil dyes and colors. An example of this is that if a cloth is dipped into water, it is cleansed by it, <margin>Water does not color.</margin> and when it is dried, the water departs, and the cloth remains in its own state and in the color it was in before, except that it is cleaner. It is the opposite with oil, because if a cloth is dipped in it, it is not separated from it by the heat of fire or air, unless it is destroyed entirely.

# THE ROSARY

<margin>The extraction of the soul.</margin>
The oil cannot be separated from the cloth itself except through washing and the drying action of fire. Water, however, is the spirit <note>In alchemy, "spirit" often refers to a volatile substance or vapor, while "water" refers to the solvent used in the process.</note> which extracts this soul from the bodies. When the soul is truly extracted from these bodies, it remains carried within that spirit, just as the dye of the dyers is carried by water onto a cloth. Then, the water recedes through drying, and the dye remains fixed in the cloth because of its oiliness. In this same way, the water is the spirit in which the tincture <note>original: "tinctura"; the essence or coloring principle that transforms base metal into gold</note> of the air is carried. When this is brought back upon the white foliated earth <term>white foliated earth: a purified, flaky metallic state reached during the alchemical process</term>, the spiritual water is immediately dried, and the soul—which is the tincture of the air—remains in the body. Therefore, the spirit retains the soul just as the soul retains the body, since the soul does not dwell in the body except by the mediation of the spirit. When they are truly joined, they may never be separated, because the spirit retains the soul just as the soul retains the earth. Hence Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> commands that the souls in the stones be venerated, for their dwelling is within them, and they are the retainers of fugitive things <note>volatile substances that evaporate easily</note> when with them. Therefore, this is our coagulation <note>the process of turning a liquid into a solid</note>, because they retain that which is fleeing. Sow, therefore, the soul into the white foliated earth, because the earth itself retains it, since

Those things which are sublimated are done so in two ways: either by themselves because they are spirits, or with others because they incorporate themselves with spirits. <margin>Three leaves.</margin> For mercury, since it is a spirit, is sublimated by itself; however, our earth, since it is a lime <note>original: "calx" - a powder produced by heating a substance</note>, is not sublimated unless it incorporates itself with mercury. ## THE CHAPTER OF GEBER
### seventy-ninth, from the
### third book.

For the preparation of the Solar medicine <note>The "Solar medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone capable of transmuting metals into gold.</note>, let there be an addition of non-burning sulfur, by way of fixing and calcining <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile impurities.</note> with the diligence of skill, perfectly administered. Apply also a manifold method of solution, with much reiteration until it becomes pure. This is indeed achieved through a perfect administration which is completed by sublimation <note>Sublimation is the process where a solid turns directly into vapor and then back to solid, used here to purify the substance.</note>. And the method of this addition is through the reiteration of the part of the non-fixed stone of sublimation, joining it with ingenuity until it is elevated with it, and repeatedly fixed with it so that it remains stable. And when the order of this abundance of completion is reiterated many times, the abundance of this medicine is multiplied all the more, its quality is further increased, and the growth of its perfection is greatly multiplied.

<margin>Summary of the work.</margin>
And indeed, lest we be bitten by the impious <note>A common alchemical trope: writing in riddles or brevity to prevent the "unworthy" from discovering the secret.</note>, we relate the entire completion of this mastery <term>Magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> in a brief, complete, and well-known discourse.

And its intention is that, by the method of sublimation, the stone and its addition may be most perfectly cleansed.

<margin>The addition.</margin>
And from this point, by the method of ingenious skills, let the volatile among them be fixed. Then, truly, let the fixed be made volatile.

# THE ROSE GARDEN

Whether the effect is improved through distillation, we have sufficiently treated the cleansing and purification of those things with which the imperfect bodies <note>The "imperfect bodies" usually refer to base metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron, which the alchemist seeks to transform into "perfect" gold or silver.</note> can be prepared, purified, improved, and refined—always by means of the appropriate fire. For they are prepared and purified by these means, according to the intention of the fire, in this manner. For these imperfect bodies possess superfluous humidities and a combustible sulfurousness <note>In alchemical theory, metals were thought to be composed of varying purity of Sulfur and Mercury; "combustible sulfur" was seen as an impurity that caused metals to tarnish or burn.</note> which generates blackness when mixed into them, corrupting the aforementioned bodies. These and such things are the superfluities in these aforementioned bodies, which have been discovered in them through our experience and certain, ingenious investigation. And because these superfluities happen to these bodies accidentally <note>The author distinguishes between "accidental" impurities (which can be removed) and the "radical" or essential nature of the metal.</note> and not radically, the stripping away of these accidents is therefore possible.

<margin>This is the preparation of the first stone</margin>

It therefore behooves us, with artificial fire, to cleanse these aforementioned things and to take away all accidental superfluities, so that only the substance of the <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti uiui" – Mercury, considered the "mother" of all metals.</note> and the radical sulfur remains. This constitutes the entire preparation of the imperfect things and their perfect purification. In general, the method is this: first, all the superfluous and corrupt moisture within their essence must be raised up <note>evaporated or sublimated</note> with a proportional fire, as well as the subtle and burning superfluity. This is done by **calcining** <margin>Calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or cause oxidation.</note></margin>. Then, the total remaining corrupt substance within that lime <note>original: "calce"; the powdery residue left after heating</note>—consisting of burning moisture and blackness—must be eroded away with the aforementioned cleansed corrosive, sharp, or bitter substances. This continues until the lime becomes white or red, or is colored and cleansed according to the body’s nature and properties, and is pure from all the previously mentioned superfluity or corruption. These substances are cleansed with these corrosives by grinding, soaking <margin>Cleansing</margin>, and washing. Afterward, the total unclean earthiness and the combustible, thick foulness must be destroyed or cast down. This is done using the aforementioned cleansed or pure things that do not possess metallic fusion <note>substances that do not melt into metal themselves</note>, mixed and well-ground with the aforementioned lime (which has been purified in the manner described). During the fusion or the reduction of the lime, these agents will retain the thick and unclean earthiness within themselves <margin>Separation</margin>, while the body remains pure, cleansed of every corrupting superfluity.

## CONCERNING THE WAXING
### of the white elixir.

<margin>Waxing <note>original: "Ceratio." The process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency to aid its fusion with metals.</note></margin>
From this point, therefore, extract the crystalline plate which you will find shining at the bottom; first, grind it and soften it with the final waxing. This is done by dropping onto it, drop by drop, while in the crucible over a light fire, some of its own "white air" <note>original: "aere albo." Likely referring to a distilled spirit or volatile substance previously mentioned.</note> already described, until it melts like wax without smoke. Then, test it upon a glowing hot plate: if it dissolves as swiftly as wax, it is properly waxed. Making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note></margin> of all the philosophers: that when you have fixed the sublimated parts <note>Substances purified by heating into vapor and then solidifying.</note>, you should return the purest part of the earth and repeat the sublimation of the remaining non-fixed part over that which is fixed, until it likewise becomes fixed. From here, test it over the fire; if it yields a good fusion, then you have sufficiently repeated the sublimation. If not, repeat the sublimation of the non-fixed part over it time after time, until it melts quickly like wax without smoke; then extract it and allow it to cool. From the aforementioned chapter, note carefully the zealous intention of the author in that he repeats the method of waxing so many times. Perhaps it would have been enough to have repeated it once, but he did so in order to impress more strongly and tenaciously upon the reader's intellect the necessity of the tireless multiplication of the waxing; therefore

<margin>The diverse regimen of the work.</margin>
To act. To dissolve the coarse into the simple and to refine it; to wash away the dark into the light; to lead back the moist into the dry; and to fix the volatile upon the fixed body. To dissolve <term>Soluere: the process of breaking down a solid into its liquid or primary state</term> is to divide the bodies and to create the first matter or nature. To wash <term>Abluere: purification through liquid</term> is to bury, to distill, and to calcine <note>To reduce a substance to powder through heat</note>. To lead back <term>Reducere: restoring or concentrating a substance</term> is to enrich, to wax, or to impregnate and refine. To fix <term>Figere: making a volatile substance resistant to heat</term> is to betroth <note>original: "desponsare," a metaphor for the chemical union of substances</note>, to resolve, and to coagulate. # THE ROSARY

<margin>The third step or order.</margin>
But the Stone is also administered in a third step, which consists of the final completion of the preparation; namely, that you now make the fixed Stone volatile <note>In alchemy, "fixed" means solid or resistant to fire, while "volatile" means able to be vaporized or transformed into spirit.</note> through the methods of sublimation, and sublime it with non-fixed spirits. To sublime the fixed is nothing other than to convert the body into spirit. This secret is extracted from the sayings of the philosopher as follows: for in the thirty-seventh chapter it is held that a spirit is not mixed with a body—that is, a fixed substance, whatever it may be—unless it is first treated with the mastery <note>original: "magisterio," referring to the specialized alchemical process or "The Magistery."</note>; that is, the Stone must first be dissolved and then coagulated. But you ask, how is the Stone

<margin>What kind of solution.</margin>
dissolved? It must be said that it is done with sharp waters <note>original: "aquis acutis," likely referring to mineral acids or strong solvents.</note> possessing pungency and sharpness without dregs, such as wine vinegar, etc. If, however, you ask why the Stone is dissolved, it must be said (as held in chapter thirty-seven) that everything which is dissolved acquires the nature of salts and alums, because only salts are melted

<margin>Salts are melted.</margin>
before they are turned into glass; and similarly, according to their own nature, only these salts are dissolved. Therefore, if our Stone is dissolved, it will acquire the nature of salts. But that which is melted enters in, and whatever enters in transmutes, etc. In chapter fifty-seven it is held that bodies are sublimated through the most excellent degree of fire, until the fixed is totally raised with the non-fixed. As in chapter twelve: if the whole has not been sublimated, let a quantity of the non-fixed part be added to it again, until it is sufficient for a total elevation.

# OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.

No higher being can be born above him,
Whether by art or through nature’s power,
From any living creature in this hour.
The philosophers call him their own son,
He can accomplish all that they have done.
Whatever a human may desire from his hand,
He grants health quickly throughout the land.
Gold, silver, and precious stones so bright,
Strength, youth, beauty, and pure light.
Anger, sorrow, poverty, and sickness he turns away,
Blessed is the man to whom God grants this day.

### The Response of Queen Luna.

Here is born the noble Empress of great wealth,
All philosophers call her their daughter in health.
She multiplies and brings forth children without end,
They are immortal, pure, and without stain, my friend.
She drives away death and holds poverty in hate,
She grants riches, health, honor, and a happy state.
And she surpasses gold, silver, and jewels so fine,
All medicines, both the great and the small design.
Nothing on earth is equal to her worth,
For this we thank God, who rules heaven and earth.

->Geber<- <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a legendary 8th-century Islamic alchemist whose writings formed the foundation of European alchemy.</note>: Truly, in our investigation, by which we are certain and have considered through manifest experience, all the words are true which have now been written by us alone in our volumes, according to what we have seen through experiment and reason reduced into these volumes; those things, indeed, which we have extracted with our fingers through our own experience, and seen with our eyes, and touched with our hands, we have written in the summary of our perfection of the mastery. <note>original Latin: "Inuestigatione vero nostra qua certi sumus... scripsimus in sumā nostri perfectionis magisterij."</note>

<margin>Scattered intention.</margin>
Therefore, let the wise <term>artisan</term> <note>Latin: *artifex*; refers to the alchemist as a skilled maker or craftsman</note> study within our volumes by gathering together our scattered intention, which we have set forth in various places so that it might not be made public to the wicked or the ignorant. Let him test what he has gathered until, through the persistence of labor, he arrives at a total <term>understanding</term> <note>Latin: *cognitio*; a deep, experiential knowledge</note> by studying and <term>experimenting</term> <note>Latin: *experimentando*; implies both physical testing and personal experience</note> with ingenuity. Let the artisan, therefore, exert himself, and he shall find it. But so that we ourselves are not bitten by the envious, we declare that we have not handed down our <term>knowledge</term> <note>Latin: *scientia*</note> in a continuous discourse; rather, we have scattered it in different chapters. We have done this because if it had been handed down continuously, the upright and the wicked alike would have seized upon it unworthily. Similarly, we have hidden it even where we have spoken most openly; yet we have not spoken in riddles,
<margin>Scattered knowledge.</margin>
but have addressed the artisan in a plain series of words. We have recorded it in such a manner of speech that its gathering together happens only by the mind of God—the most high and blessed, sublime and glorious—and by our own mind, we who wrote it, or by the infusion of the goodness of divine grace, which God grants to or withholds from whom He wills. Therefore, let the
<margin>Consolation.</margin>
<term>son of the doctrine</term> <note>A traditional alchemical term for a dedicated student or initiate</note> not despair, for if he seeks it, he shall find it—not by the doctrine alone, but by the investigation of the movement of his own <term>nature</term>. For he who seeks through the goodness of his own industry shall find knowledge; but he who seeks only through the pursuit of books shall arrive most slowly at this most precious art, because we have published this art, investigated by ourselves, for ourselves alone.
